Shinmeisai May 5 |map = {{location map|Japan Yamanashi|lat_deg=35|lat_min=29|lat_sec=41.3|lon_deg=138|lon_min=48|lon_sec=11.4|label=冨士山下宮小室浅間神社|position=bottom|width=200|float=center|caption=|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=20}} {{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=11|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|coord={{coord|35|29|41.36|N|138|48|11.40|E}}}} }} '''{{illOmuro Sengen Shrine (Yamanashi)|lt=Omuro Sengen Shrine|ja|冨士山下宮小室浅間神社}}''' (冨士山下宮小室浅間神社[[ja:冨士山下宮小室浅間神社]]) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Fujiyoshida|ja|富士吉田市}}, {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|ja|山梨県}}. The former rank under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ja|近代rank制度}} was that of a Gōsha, and it is now designated as a Beppyo Shrine under the jurisdiction of the {{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|ja|神社本庁}}. It is one of the many {{ill|Sengen shrines|ja|浅間神社}} across Japan. The former name was '''Fuji San Shimomiya Sengen Shrine'''慶応四年辰年八月の「富士山下宮社地取調書上帳」. The registered name as a religious corporation is '''Komuro Sengen Shrine''' (おむろせんげんじんじゃ). The shrine is dedicated to the {{ill|Ubusunagami|ja|産土神}} of the Fuji Hokuroku region and the entire {{ill|Fujiyoshida|ja|富士吉田市}}, serving as the {{ill|Sōchinju|ja|総鎮守}} of the three villages of Kamiyoshida, Shimoyoshida, and Matsuyama. {{ill|Shinme|ja|神馬}} are kept at the shrine. Locally, it is also referred to as "Shimomiya-san" or "Shimosengen." == Overview == Throughout the year, divination ('''占い''') and oracles ('''神籤(おみくじ）''') play a significant role in the festivals held at the shrine. This includes the "Horse Hoof Divination Yabusame festival" and the "Tsutsukayū festival," which reflect the ancient Fuji worship deeply rooted in the lives of local residents. According to the {{ill|Kai Kokushi|ja|甲斐国志}}, the shrine is the birthplace deity of Kamiyoshida, Shimoyoshida, and Matsuyama villages. Even as other shrines have increased in the surrounding area, the practice of {{ill|Hatsumiya Mairi|ja|初宮参り}} for newborns remains strong, indicating the deep faith of local residents. == Deities == * {{ill|Konohanasakuya-hime|ja|コノハナノサクヤビメ}} == History == According to the shrine legend, in Enryaku 12 (793), {{ill|Sakanoue no Tamuramaro|ja|坂上田村麻呂}}, during his eastern expedition, prayed for victory while worshipping Mount Fuji from Yoshida. After his victory, in gratitude for the divine favor, he built the shrine in Daidō 2 (807). Early records mention the shrine as "Miya" (宮). Until the detailed village survey book of Hōei 3 (1708), it was recorded as "Sengen Miya." Originally, the settlement of Shimoyoshida was located in present-day Shimoyoshida Higashimachi, where it was enshrined at the current location of the {{ill|Higashimachi Kotohira Shrine|ja|東町金毘羅神社}}. Due to frequent snowmelt damage, the settlement and shrine were relocated to their current location, backed by the Kenmaruo Lava Flow{{Cite book|title=下吉田の民俗|date=1990.3.25|year=1990|publisher=富士吉田市教育委員会}}. In Kenmu 2 (1355) on September 23, the head of {{ill|Prince Moriyoshi|ja|護良親王}}, a descendant of Emperor Seiwa, was buried at the root of a sacred katsura tree, and a petition was left behind. In Tenshō 4 (1576), the towns of both Kamiyoshida and Shimoyoshida were completely burned down during the battle between the {{ill|Hōjō clan|ja|北条氏}} and {{ill|Oyamada clan|ja|小山田氏}} ({{ill|Katsuyama-ki|ja|勝山記}}). During the Edo period, the shrine was also the guardian of the largest temple in the Fuji Hokuroku area, {{ill|Gekko-ji|ja|月江寺}}, and until the Meiji era, recitations by Gekko-ji monks were part of the shrine festivals. In Kan'ei 3 (1626) on April 6, a sacred ancient cedar tree in the shrine grounds was struck by lightning and burned ({{ill|Kai Kokushi|ja|甲斐国志}}). A fragment of this tree is displayed as a plaque in the current haiden. The haiden dates back to the Tenshō era (1573-1593). The honden, built by {{ill|Gunai Daiku Nakama|ja|郡内大工仲間}} master carpenter Kayanuma Yasaburō in Meiwa 4 (1767), is the largest single-bay shrine building in Yamanashi Prefecture. This honden served as a model for subsequent shrine buildings in the area. Although it is not registered as a cultural property, it is significant in its architecture. [[File:Fujisan Simomiya Omurosengen Jinjya 冨士山下宮小室浅間神社 本殿.jpg|thumb|250x250px|Honden. Single-bay Irimoya-zukuri style with Karahafu at the front. It is the largest single-bay honden in Yamanashi Prefecture. The eaves are enclosed with covering walls.]] During the Meiji period, the shrine transferred its parishioner area of Kamiyoshida to the {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongū Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮冨士浅間神社}} and changed its name from "Fuji San Shimomiya Sengen Shrine" to the current "Komuro Sengen Shrine." In line with this change, the enshrined deities were unified from "Sengen Daimyōjin, Amaterasu Ōmikami, Inukai Daimyōjin, Aitaka Daigongen, Shinra Saburō Yoshimitsu (Prince Moriyoshi)" to "Konohanasakuya-hime (Sengen Ōkami)." The shrine crest was also changed from "Shuro no Ha" to "Yamato Yaezakura." Amaterasu Ōmikami was moved to the Gosha Shrine, and Prince Moriyoshi was enshrined separately in the Daitōmiya Shrine. In 1957, the shrine exchanged its grounds and municipal land on Otaruyama with the neighboring Shimoyoshida First Elementary School for playground expansion. In the same year, it was designated a Beppyo Shrine. === Origin of the name "Shimomiya" === The term "Shimomiya" refers to the lower shrine in relation to Mount Fuji, with no specific upper shrine. There are several theories as to why it is called "Shimomiya." # Originally referred to simply as "Miya," it was called "Shimomiya" to distinguish it from other Sengen shrines that began to enshrine Sengen Ōkami in the villages, referring to the shrine lower in relation to Mount Fuji{{Cite web|和書|title=富士山下宮小室浅間神社　由諸|url=http://www.fgo.jp/~yabusame/rekisi.htm|website=www.fgo.jp|accessdate=2019-09-09}}. # The term "Shimomiya" was used by people around Lake Kawaguchi to refer to the Fuji Yoshida area, distinguishing it from {{ill|Kawaguchi Sengen Shrine|ja|河口浅間神社}}. # The term "Shimomiya" referred to the lower shrine in relation to the Komuro Sengen Shrine at the second station of Mount Fuji (now the former main shrine of the {{ill|Fuji Omuro Sengen Shrine|ja|冨士御室浅間神社}}). This theory, however, has been widely spread but is now considered a folk belief, as shown by the following points: #* Both shrines have different origins and histories. #* The {{ill|Kai Kokushi|ja|甲斐国志}} mentions the Komuro Sengen Shrine's satomiya in Katsuyama, but there is no mention of the relationship with Shimomiya Sengen. #* The Komuro Sengen Shrine at the second station was easily acquired by Katsuyama in Fujikawaguchiko as an exclave. #* The shrine building from the second station was moved to the satomiya grounds in Katsuyama. #* The relationship with the Komuro Sengen Shrine at the second station was not proven, so it was excluded from the list of components for the Mount Fuji World Cultural Heritage designation (it was seen more as a birthplace, tutelary, or guardian deity, deeply rooted in local life rather than Fuji worship). #* During the Meiji period, another shrine in the same city, Ōasumi's {{ill|Komuro Sengen Shrine (Fujiyoshida Ōasumi)|ja|小室浅間神社 (富士吉田市大明見)}}, was renamed to "Komuro Sengen Shrine." #* The Yabusame festival was traditionally held together, but the records and descriptions, such as the {{ill|Katsuyama-ki|ja|勝山記}} and {{ill|Myōhō-ji-ki|ja|妙法寺記}}, do not mention horse hoof divination or divination rituals in Katsuyama. #* The place where the Yabusame was held is described as "Rokubanba near Nakano Chaya" in theory 3, but it is actually "Nakano Chaya near the second station," which is far apart, showing no connection between Rokubanba and the Komuro Sengen Shrine at the second station. #* The Yabusame was performed by various shrines and villages in the Fuji Hokuroku area. Over time, the Rokubanba became the Nagabanba, and the ceremonies became more localized. #* As mentioned below, there is confusion between "Shimomiya" and "Shimoyashima." === Confusion between "Shimoyashima" and "Shimomiya" === In {{ill|Fujiyoshida|ja|富士吉田市}}, the {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongū Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮冨士浅間神社}} is located in Kamiyoshida, while the Komuro Sengen Shrine is in Shimoyoshida. Therefore, it is easy to mistake the Komuro Sengen Shrine as the "Shimomiya" in contrast to the "Hongū" of Kitaguchi. In modern times, the Kitaguchi Hongū is referred to as "Kami Sengen" or "Kami Sen," and the Komuro Sengen Shrine as "Shimoyashima" or "Shimo Sen," which further perpetuates the confusion. However, '''"Shimoyashima" originally referred to the {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongū Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮冨士浅間神社}} rather than the Fuji San Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine'''{{Cite web|和書|url=https://www.pref.yamanashi.jp/fujisan/rebirth/documents/fujisanmichi-omote.pdf|title=富士参詣富士山道表|accessdate=2019.02|publisher=山梨県富士山世界文化遺産保存活用推進協議会}}. For example, the 'Hachiyō Kunsun-zu' from Enpō 8 (1680), which depicts the Yoshida Route to Mount Fuji, refers to the current Kitaguchi Hongū grounds as "Shimoyashima"{{Cite journal|author=串田優子 伊藤裕久|year=2006|title=北口本宮冨士浅間神社境内空間の変遷過程|journal=日本建築学会計画系論文集|volume=第604号|page=159−16S}}. Additionally, the 'Kai Kokushi' from Bunka 11 (1814) describes the Komuro Sengen Shrine at the second station (now Fuji Omuro Sengen Shrine) as "Kami Sengen," and the shrine at Kitaguchi as "Shimoyashima," with the shrine at Shimoyoshida referred to as "Shimomiya Sengen." From the above, it is clear that "Shimoyashima" and "Shimomiya Sengen" were separate entities. However, after the transfer of the parishioner area of Kamiyoshida to Kitaguchi Hongū, the relationship with the Komuro Sengen Shrine at the second station in Katsuyama of Fujikawaguchiko weakened. Thus, the term "Kami Sengen" ceased to be used for the second station shrine, leading to the Kitaguchi Hongū being referred to as "Kami Sengen" and the Komuro Sengen Shrine as "Shimoyashima," with the latter being renamed to "Komuro Sengen Shrine" during the Meiji period, further perpetuating the confusion between "Shimoyashima" and "Shimomiya." == festivals == === Yabusame festival === [[File:小室浅間神社（下宮）神馬舎.jpg|thumb|200px|Shinmesha and the Shinme kept in it]] [[File:Fujiyosida-Yabusame-FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengen.webm|thumb|Yabusame at Fuji San Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine, taken on September 19, 2020]] The Yabusame festival, designated as an Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Yamanashi Prefecture, is held on September 19, the day of the {{ill|Reisai|ja|festival}}, and is famous for the "Horse Hoof Divination" (''batei uranai''). Locally known as "Umatobakashi" (甲州弁: to run the horse), the Yabusame festival is said to have started with a mid-period horseback riding in Chōkan 2 (1164), with the formal Yabusame festival beginning in Angen 2 (1176). The formal practices of the festival, including Asauma (morning horse) and Yuuma (evening horse), were established in Kenkyū 3 (1192), and the festival date was set to September 19 in Eikyō 12 (1440). In the shrine grounds, the sacred horses used for Yabusame are kept. These horses are donated by the Japan Racing Association. This festival is unique from the generally known Yabusame, being closely tied to agricultural faith and the lives of local residents. It features divination by "Ura-bito" (diviners) who interpret the horse hoof prints (batei uranai), oracles (mikuji) to seek divine will, and a week-long purification ritual called "kiribi." The horses for Yabusame are donated by parishioners, and the festival begins with the application and selection of the horses, known as "Uma-dashi no Kushi-uranai," held on January 15, the day after the Tsutsukayū festival. The festival includes the "Hatsu-ma-zoroi" on September 1, "Naka-ma-zoroi" on September 9, "Kessai-hajime" on September 13, "Ato-ma-zoroi" on September 15, "Tenjinsha-sankō and Tenjinsha Sannō-sai" on September 18, the "Reitaisai Yabusame Matsuri" on September 19, and the "Ato-matsuri" on September 20. In the past, families without horses would borrow them from local or neighboring farmers. However, with the decline in horse ownership, the shrine now keeps horses for the festival. Originally held at the "Rokubanba near Nakano Chaya," halfway between the Mount Fuji climbing gate and Umagaeshi, the festival has been performed at the "Honmachi Nakamu Ra Horse Grounds" since the late Edo period. The current horse grounds were used by 1848, as shown in the "festival map of September 19" from that year. [[File:富士山神輿.JPG|200px|thumb|right|Fuji Mountain Mikoshi]] In 2007, after a hiatus, the Fuji Mountain Mikoshi was revived, and its procession takes place on the eve of the festival, September 18. ; Uma-dashi no Kushi-uranai (Horse Selection Divination) : Early morning on January 15, after the results of the Tsutsukayū festival divination are announced, the application for Yabusame horses begins. The horse owners and horses are selected through a divination ritual held at noon. Traditionally, 30 to 60 applications were made for the six horses, and being selected as a horse owner was a great honor. Recently, the number of applications has been lower than the required number. ; Hatsu-ma-zoroi (First Horse Gathering) : On September 1, all horses for the festival gather at the shrine, where a ritual is performed. Each horse owner draws a lot for the practice saddle and receives a set of practice horse gear from the diviners. The horses are then shown to the public and trained (currently, the sacred horses kept at the shrine practice in the shrine grounds). ; Naka-ma-zoroi (Middle Horse Gathering) : On September 9, the horses gather again for a ritual and practice runs. ; Kessai-hajime (Start of Purification) : On September 13, a ritual is held where the scroll with the image of Konohanasakuya-hime and sacred branches are bestowed. The horse owners and participants then enter a purification period and stay in the shrine's purification hall. Previously, this was done at each horse owner's home, where the family, except for the participants, would leave, and a temporary altar was set up for a period of purification. ; Ato-ma-zoroi (Final Horse Gathering) : On September 15, the horses are adorned with decorations, and the participants draw lots for the actual saddle. The diviners then bestow the necessary horse gear for the festival. ; Sannō-sha Yoimiya-sai (Sannō Shrine festival Eve) : On September 17, the participants visit Sannō Shrine for the bow-taking ceremony, where they receive instructions from the diviners. ; Sannō-sha-sai & Yabusame Matsuri Yoimiya-sai (Sannō Shrine festival & Yabusame festival Eve) : On September 18, the priests, diviners, horse owners, and related participants form a procession to Sannō Shrine, and the Fuji Mountain Mikoshi is carried. : That night, a lottery is held to determine the roles of the horses and the order of their runs for the festival the next day. : The horse gear is managed by the "Ura-bito" (diviners), and the decorative "Otenkō" placed on the horse's forehead is woven from the horse's mane and is believed to be a continuation of the horn-shaped decorations seen on horse-shaped haniwa. [[File:馬蹄占流鏑馬.jpg|thumb|278x278px|Yūma running. The horn-shaped decoration on the horse's forehead is called "Otenkō"]] ; Reitaisai Yabusame Matsuri (festival Yabusame festival) : On September 19, arrows, bows, and targets are given to the horse owners, and the Yabusame is performed in the order of Asauma (morning horse) and Yūma (evening horse), followed by the hoof print divination (batei uranai). The festival concludes with the "San'nō-san's Noppalai" (San'nō's farewell run), where the mountain deity is sent back to the mountain after overseeing the autumn harvest. ; Yabusame Ato-matsuri (Yabusame After festival) : On September 20, the results of the hoof print divination are announced and promptly conveyed to each town. ; Ohimaichi : After the Yabusame festival, the priests visit each town for the "Ohimaichi" ritual based on the divination results. : The ritual is held in various locations, from small gatherings of nearby households to larger events at dining halls or community centers. An altar is set up with the deity's scroll, and participants share food and drink. : In each household, a paper talisman from the priest is received to ensure a year free from fires and disputes. === Tsutsukayū festival === [[File:FujisanSimomiyaOmuroSengenShrine Kayu-ura Ritual.jpg|thumb|Tsutsukayū festival conducted overnight by the hereditary diviner family ({{ill|Yoshi no Ike Onsen|ja|葭之池温泉}})]] In Yamanashi Prefecture, the Tsutsukayū festival is held at various shrines in the Fuji Hokuroku and Yatsugatake regions. At Komuro Sengen Shrine, the Tsutsukayū festival is held overnight from January 14 to early morning January 15. The ritual predicts the year's harvest, weather, sericulture, and the number of Fuji pilgrims, with a notable focus on the latterKatsumata (2007), p.643. The results are published as the Tsutsukayū Divination Mark. After the Tsutsukayū ritual, another divination known as "Terifuri Divination" is performed, where a "Katsunoki" (Nured) piece is placed on the embers and its burning pattern is observed to predict the weather. These results are also published. The Tsutsukayū ritual has been documented in the Sengoku-era diary "Katsuyama-ki" as "Tsutsukai," showing that it has remained largely unchanged since thenKatsumata (2007), p.644. The Tsutsukayū ritual is performed by a hereditary diviner family ({{ill|Yoshi no Ike Onsen|ja|葭之池温泉}}). === Okoe-sai (Changing of the deity's Garments) === Every 60 years, the "Okoe-sai" is held to change the garments of the deity (Konohanasakuya-hime). In the 20th century, this ritual was held in 1950 (Shōwa 25). In the Heisei era, it was held on September 19, 2010 (Heisei 22), and the next ritual is scheduled for 2070. It is believed that seeing the deity outside of this ritual brings misfortune. === Shinmeisai (Sacred Horse festival) === Held annually on Children's Day, May 5, it is known as the "festival of Horses and Children." The festival includes gratitude and memorial services for working horses and past sacred horses, and it features stalls and events from local businesses. == Sacred Horses == [[File:冨士山下宮小室浅間神社 JRA奉納 神馬 瑞桜（ヒカリシャーク）.jpg|thumb|Sacred horse 瑞桜 (Hikari Shark)]] Since 1993, sacred horses have been kept at the shrine to maintain and preserve the Yabusame festival and the hoof print divination ritual. {| class="wikitable" |+History of Sacred Horses ! No. ! Horse name ! Sacred Horse name ! Notes |- | 1 | Hikari Shark | 瑞桜 (Zuio) | |- | 2 | Maxport | | |- | 3 | Towa Takeshiba | | |- | 4 | Daiichi Hijiri | | |- | 5 | Tokin | | |- | 6 | Ichiei Clipper | | |- | 7 | Shiro | | |- | 8 | Kings of the Sun | 旺輝 (Ōki) | |- | 9 | Wise Selection | 賢旺 (Kenō) | Current |} The sacred horses, after their lifetime service, are enshrined in the sacred horse shrine. Every year on May 5, the Shinmeisai is held. In addition to the sacred horses, the shrine also keeps Kiso horses and ponies. == Sessha and Massha == === Daitōmiya Shrine and Hinazuru Shrine === * Deities: {{ill|Prince Moriyoshi|ja|護良親王}} and {{ill|Princess Hinazuru|ja|雛鶴姫}} * festival: May 10 (Katsura festival) [[File:Ootounomiya-katura1.jpg|thumb|216px|Sacred Katsura Tree beside the main shrine, known as the "Daitōmiya Katsura Shrine"]] In the shrine grounds, the sacred Katsura tree, known as "Daitōmiya Katsura Shrine," is revered as a deity. According to ancient documents, in the turmoil of the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, the severed head of {{ill|Prince Moriyoshi|ja|護良親王}} was buried at the root of the sacred Katsura tree by Princess Hinazuru. One such document is a copy of a petition dated September 23, Kenmu 2 (1355), from a descendant of Emperor Seiwa. It describes the burial of Prince Moriyoshi's head at the root of the sacred Katsura tree in the shrine grounds and requests that an image of {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshimitsu|ja|源義光}} be carved and secretly worshipped as Prince Moriyoshi alongside the tree. [[File:Ootounomiya-katura2.jpg|thumb|From right to left: Hinazuru Shrine, Daitōmiya Shrine, Head Mound]] The sacred Katsura tree, estimated to be about 800 years old, is designated a natural monument of Fujiyoshida City. === Shinme Shrine === * deity: White Horse Spirit * festival: May 5 (Shinmeisai) The shrine is dedicated to the sacred horse and the spirits of past horses. The Shinmeisai held on May 5 is known as the "festival of Horses," featuring stalls from local businesses and horse riding experiences for children. === Hie Shrine === * deity: {{ill|Ōyamakui|ja|大山咋神}} * festival: May 5 Locally known as the "Monkey Shrine," the shrine features statues of monkeys, which are believed to be divine messengers. === Gosha Shrine (Daishin Shrine, Yama Shrine, Tennō Shrine, Inari Shrine, Tenjin Shrine) === * Deities: Amaterasu Ōmikami, Ōyamatsumi, Susanoo-no-Mikoto, Ōkuninushi, Sukunabikona, Ukanomitama, Sugawara no Michizane * festival: April 10 The shrine combines five shrines into one. === Ebisu Shrine === * deity: {{ill|Ebisu (mythology)|ja|えびす}} * festival: November 19 (Ebisu-kō) The shrine features an Ebisu statue in the style of Ogata Kōrin. The Ebisu-kō festival is held on November 19. === Benzaiten Shrine === * deity: {{ill|Benzaiten|ja|弁才天}} An ancient shrine utilizing a lava tree mold, preserving an old form of Mount Fuji worship. Surrounded by Maruishi stones. === Arata Hachiman Shrine === * Deities: {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ja|応神天皇}}, {{ill|Tama Yorihime|ja|タマヨリビメ (日向神話)}}, {{ill|Empress Jingū|ja|神功皇后}}, Tanabe Ichike ancestor spirits === Suitengu Shrine === * Deities: Amenominakanushi, Emperor Antoku, Takakura Hirashin no Miya (Kenreimon-in, {{ill|Taira no Tokiko|ja|平徳子}}), Nii no Ama ({{ill|Taira no Tokiko|ja|平時子}}) File:Fuji-omurosengen-horse.jpg|Shinme Shrine, sacred horse statue File:Fuji-omurosengen-monkey.jpg|Hie Shrine "See no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil" statues File:FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengenJinja Benten.jpg|Benzaiten Shrine and Maruishi stones File:FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengenJinja ebisu.jpg|Ebisu Shrine File:FujisanSimomiya OmurosengenJinja Gosya.jpg|Gosha Shrine, five-bay structure, remodeled in the Shōwa era File:FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengenJinja suitengu.jpg|Suitengu Shrine File:FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengenJinja aratahatimangu2.jpg|Arata Hachiman Shrine Haiden File:FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengenJinja aratahatimangu.jpg|Arata Hachiman Shrine Honden File:FujisanSimomiya OmuroSengenjinja Gaku.jpg|Great Torii plaque, calligraphy by {{ill|Tokugawa Munetaka|ja|徳川宗敬}}, 1981 (Shōwa 56) File:FujisanSimomiya OmurosengenJinja torii.jpg|Great Torii, completed in 1981 (Shōwa 56), collapsed in 2004 (Heisei 16) due to a typhoon, rebuilt using original materials in 2010 (Heisei 22), with the pillars replaced with steel in 2020 (Reiwa 2) due to severe damage File:Fujisan Simomiya OmuroSengen Jinja Gaku Sindaisugi.jpg|Shindai-sugi plaque in the Haiden, made from a fragment of a sacred ancient cedar struck by lightning in Tenbun and Kan'ei eras, preserved as recorded in Kai Kokushi File:FujisanSimomiyaOmuroSengenJinja Temizu.jpg|Temizuya, built in 1933 (Shōwa 8) to commemorate the birth of Crown Prince Akihito File:FujisanSimomiyaOmuroSengenJinja KaguraDen.jpg|Kagura-den, built in 1975 (Shōwa 50). A rare stage-style Kagura-den in the area, built to accommodate traditional village Kabuki in place of the district's lack of Kagura File:FujisanSimomiya OmurosengenJinja.jpg|Shrine office, an Edo-period building originally used as a village hall, later moved to the shrine grounds and remodeled into the shrine office. A rotating stage and timber framework remain under the tatami mats in the hall. File:Fuji-omurosengen-pond.jpg|Sacred pond == External Shrines == The Fuji San Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine has two exclave grounds where the Konpira Shrine and Shiroō Shrine are enshrined. === Konpira Shrine === * deity: {{ill|Ōmononushi|ja|大物主}} Located in Shimoyoshida Higashimachi, Fujiyoshida City. This area is known as Furuyoshida Morigumi and is said to be the former site of the Fuji San Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine. During the Sengoku period, there was a purification site for Fuji climbers, where spring water was used for cleansing. A checkpoint was also established here to collect tolls, and it marked the starting point for the Yoshida Route to Mount Fuji, as indicated by the "First Step" stone monument. Gekkōji Temple Aizen and FujisanSimomiya Omurosengen KotohiraShrine.jpg|Konpira Shrine of Fuji San Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine and Aizen Jizō Hall of Gekkō-ji Temple. Their proximity indicates their historical relationship. FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengen KotohiraShrine.jpg|Konpira Shrine Honden Fuji Sekisyo .jpg|Stone monuments, including the "First Step" marker indicating the starting point of the Fuji Yoshida Route, located between Konpira Shrine and Aizen Jizō Hall. === Shiroō Shrine (Shiroō Gongen Shrine) === * Deities: Ōkuninushi, Ōtoshi, Shinatobe Located midway up Otaruyama in Fujiyoshida City. About a 20-minute walk east from {{ill|Arakurayama Sengen Park|ja|新倉山浅間公園}}. The festival is held on August 6, known as the "Bug festival" (虫送り), praying for the expulsion of harmful insects and diseases from the fields and homes of Fujiyoshida. The distributed {{ill|Gohei|ja|御幣}} are placed at the entrances of fields and houses. The name Gongen is a remnant of the syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism. Until the mid-Showa period, many people would climb the mountain holding torches to attend the festival. Shinmeisai May 5 |map = {{location map|Japan Yamanashi|lat_deg=35|lat_min=29|lat_sec=41.3|lon_deg=138|lon_min=48|lon_sec=11.4|label=冨士山下宮小室浅間神社|position=bottom|width=200|float=center|caption=|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=20}} {{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=11|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|coord={{coord|35|29|41.36|N|138|48|11.40|E}}}} }} '''{{illOmuro Sengen Shrine (Yamanashi)|lt=Omuro Sengen Shrine|ja|冨士山下宮小室浅間神社}}''' (冨士山下宮小室浅間神社[[ja:冨士山下宮小室浅間神社]]) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Fujiyoshida|ja|富士吉田市}}, {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|ja|山梨県}}. The former rank under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ja|近代rank制度}} was that of a Gōsha, and it is now designated as a Beppyo Shrine under the jurisdiction of the {{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|ja|神社本庁}}. It is one of the many {{ill|Sengen shrines|ja|浅間神社}} across Japan. The former name was '''Fuji San Shimomiya Sengen Shrine'''慶応四年辰年八月の「富士山下宮社地取調書上帳」. The registered name as a religious corporation is '''Komuro Sengen Shrine''' (おむろせんげんじんじゃ). The shrine is dedicated to the {{ill|Ubusunagami|ja|産土神}} of the Fuji Hokuroku region and the entire {{ill|Fujiyoshida|ja|富士吉田市}}, serving as the {{ill|Sōchinju|ja|総鎮守}} of the three villages of Kamiyoshida, Shimoyoshida, and Matsuyama. {{ill|Shinme|ja|神馬}} are kept at the shrine. Locally, it is also referred to as "Shimomiya-san" or "Shimosengen." == Overview == Throughout the year, divination ('''占い''') and oracles ('''神籤(おみくじ）''') play a significant role in the festivals held at the shrine. This includes the "Horse Hoof Divination Yabusame festival" and the "Tsutsukayū festival," which reflect the ancient Fuji worship deeply rooted in the lives of local residents. According to the {{ill|Kai Kokushi|ja|甲斐国志}}, the shrine is the birthplace deity of Kamiyoshida, Shimoyoshida, and Matsuyama villages. Even as other shrines have increased in the surrounding area, the practice of {{ill|Hatsumiya Mairi|ja|初宮参り}} for newborns remains strong, indicating the deep faith of local residents. == Deities == * {{ill|Konohanasakuya-hime|ja|コノハナノサクヤビメ}} == History == According to the shrine legend, in Enryaku 12 (793), {{ill|Sakanoue no Tamuramaro|ja|坂上田村麻呂}}, during his eastern expedition, prayed for victory while worshipping Mount Fuji from Yoshida. After his victory, in gratitude for the divine favor, he built the shrine in Daidō 2 (807). Early records mention the shrine as "Miya" (宮). Until the detailed village survey book of Hōei 3 (1708), it was recorded as "Sengen Miya." Originally, the settlement of Shimoyoshida was located in present-day Shimoyoshida Higashimachi, where it was enshrined at the current location of the {{ill|Higashimachi Kotohira Shrine|ja|東町金毘羅神社}}. Due to frequent snowmelt damage, the settlement and shrine were relocated to their current location, backed by the Kenmaruo Lava Flow{{Cite book|title=下吉田の民俗|date=1990.3.25|year=1990|publisher=富士吉田市教育委員会}}. In Kenmu 2 (1355) on September 23, the head of {{ill|Prince Moriyoshi|ja|護良親王}}, a descendant of Emperor Seiwa, was buried at the root of a sacred katsura tree, and a petition was left behind. In Tenshō 4 (1576), the towns of both Kamiyoshida and Shimoyoshida were completely burned down during the battle between the {{ill|Hōjō clan|ja|北条氏}} and {{ill|Oyamada clan|ja|小山田氏}} ({{ill|Katsuyama-ki|ja|勝山記}}). During the Edo period, the shrine was also the guardian of the largest temple in the Fuji Hokuroku area, {{ill|Gekko-ji|ja|月江寺}}, and until the Meiji era, recitations by Gekko-ji monks were part of the shrine festivals. In Kan'ei 3 (1626) on April 6, a sacred ancient cedar tree in the shrine grounds was struck by lightning and burned ({{ill|Kai Kokushi|ja|甲斐国志}}). A fragment of this tree is displayed as a plaque in the current haiden. The haiden dates back to the Tenshō era (1573-1593). The honden, built by {{ill|Gunai Daiku Nakama|ja|郡内大工仲間}} master carpenter Kayanuma Yasaburō in Meiwa 4 (1767), is the largest single-bay shrine building in Yamanashi Prefecture. This honden served as a model for subsequent shrine buildings in the area. Although it is not registered as a cultural property, it is significant in its architecture. [[File:Fujisan Simomiya Omurosengen Jinjya 冨士山下宮小室浅間神社 本殿.jpg|thumb|250x250px|Honden. Single-bay Irimoya-zukuri style with Karahafu at the front. It is the largest single-bay honden in Yamanashi Prefecture. The eaves are enclosed with covering walls.]] During the Meiji period, the shrine transferred its parishioner area of Kamiyoshida to the {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongū Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮冨士浅間神社}} and changed its name from "Fuji San Shimomiya Sengen Shrine" to the current "Komuro Sengen Shrine." In line with this change, the enshrined deities were unified from "Sengen Daimyōjin, Amaterasu Ōmikami, Inukai Daimyōjin, Aitaka Daigongen, Shinra Saburō Yoshimitsu (Prince Moriyoshi)" to "Konohanasakuya-hime (Sengen Ōkami)." The shrine crest was also changed from "Shuro no Ha" to "Yamato Yaezakura." Amaterasu Ōmikami was moved to the Gosha Shrine, and Prince Moriyoshi was enshrined separately in the Daitōmiya Shrine. In 1957, the shrine exchanged its grounds and municipal land on Otaruyama with the neighboring Shimoyoshida First Elementary School for playground expansion. In the same year, it was designated a Beppyo Shrine. === Origin of the name "Shimomiya" === The term "Shimomiya" refers to the lower shrine in relation to Mount Fuji, with no specific upper shrine. There are several theories as to why it is called "Shimomiya." # Originally referred to simply as "Miya," it was called "Shimomiya" to distinguish it from other Sengen shrines that began to enshrine Sengen Ōkami in the villages, referring to the shrine lower in relation to Mount Fuji{{Cite web|和書|title=富士山下宮小室浅間神社　由諸|url=http://www.fgo.jp/~yabusame/rekisi.htm|website=www.fgo.jp|accessdate=2019-09-09}}. # The term "Shimomiya" was used by people around Lake Kawaguchi to refer to the Fuji Yoshida area, distinguishing it from {{ill|Kawaguchi Sengen Shrine|ja|河口浅間神社}}. # The term "Shimomiya" referred to the lower shrine in relation to the Komuro Sengen Shrine at the second station of Mount Fuji (now the former main shrine of the {{ill|Fuji Omuro Sengen Shrine|ja|冨士御室浅間神社}}). This theory, however, has been widely spread but is now considered a folk belief, as shown by the following points: #* Both shrines have different origins and histories. #* The {{ill|Kai Kokushi|ja|甲斐国志}} mentions the Komuro Sengen Shrine's satomiya in Katsuyama, but there is no mention of the relationship with Shimomiya Sengen. #* The Komuro Sengen Shrine at the second station was easily acquired by Katsuyama in Fujikawaguchiko as an exclave. #* The shrine building from the second station was moved to the satomiya grounds in Katsuyama. #* The relationship with the Komuro Sengen Shrine at the second station was not proven, so it was excluded from the list of components for the Mount Fuji World Cultural Heritage designation (it was seen more as a birthplace, tutelary, or guardian deity, deeply rooted in local life rather than Fuji worship). #* During the Meiji period, another shrine in the same city, Ōasumi's {{ill|Komuro Sengen Shrine (Fujiyoshida Ōasumi)|ja|小室浅間神社 (富士吉田市大明見)}}, was renamed to "Komuro Sengen Shrine." #* The Yabusame festival was traditionally held together, but the records and descriptions, such as the {{ill|Katsuyama-ki|ja|勝山記}} and {{ill|Myōhō-ji-ki|ja|妙法寺記}}, do not mention horse hoof divination or divination rituals in Katsuyama. #* The place where the Yabusame was held is described as "Rokubanba near Nakano Chaya" in theory 3, but it is actually "Nakano Chaya near the second station," which is far apart, showing no connection between Rokubanba and the Komuro Sengen Shrine at the second station. #* The Yabusame was performed by various shrines and villages in the Fuji Hokuroku area. Over time, the Rokubanba became the Nagabanba, and the ceremonies became more localized. #* As mentioned below, there is confusion between "Shimomiya" and "Shimoyashima." === Confusion between "Shimoyashima" and "Shimomiya" === In {{ill|Fujiyoshida|ja|富士吉田市}}, the {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongū Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮冨士浅間神社}} is located in Kamiyoshida, while the Komuro Sengen Shrine is in Shimoyoshida. Therefore, it is easy to mistake the Komuro Sengen Shrine as the "Shimomiya" in contrast to the "Hongū" of Kitaguchi. In modern times, the Kitaguchi Hongū is referred to as "Kami Sengen" or "Kami Sen," and the Komuro Sengen Shrine as "Shimoyashima" or "Shimo Sen," which further perpetuates the confusion. However, '''"Shimoyashima" originally referred to the {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongū Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮冨士浅間神社}} rather than the Fuji San Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine'''{{Cite web|和書|url=https://www.pref.yamanashi.jp/fujisan/rebirth/documents/fujisanmichi-omote.pdf|title=富士参詣富士山道表|accessdate=2019.02|publisher=山梨県富士山世界文化遺産保存活用推進協議会}}. For example, the 'Hachiyō Kunsun-zu' from Enpō 8 (1680), which depicts the Yoshida Route to Mount Fuji, refers to the current Kitaguchi Hongū grounds as "Shimoyashima"{{Cite journal|author=串田優子 伊藤裕久|year=2006|title=北口本宮冨士浅間神社境内空間の変遷過程|journal=日本建築学会計画系論文集|volume=第604号|page=159−16S}}. Additionally, the 'Kai Kokushi' from Bunka 11 (1814) describes the Komuro Sengen Shrine at the second station (now Fuji Omuro Sengen Shrine) as "Kami Sengen," and the shrine at Kitaguchi as "Shimoyashima," with the shrine at Shimoyoshida referred to as "Shimomiya Sengen." From the above, it is clear that "Shimoyashima" and "Shimomiya Sengen" were separate entities. However, after the transfer of the parishioner area of Kamiyoshida to Kitaguchi Hongū, the relationship with the Komuro Sengen Shrine at the second station in Katsuyama of Fujikawaguchiko weakened. Thus, the term "Kami Sengen" ceased to be used for the second station shrine, leading to the Kitaguchi Hongū being referred to as "Kami Sengen" and the Komuro Sengen Shrine as "Shimoyashima," with the latter being renamed to "Komuro Sengen Shrine" during the Meiji period, further perpetuating the confusion between "Shimoyashima" and "Shimomiya." == festivals == === Yabusame festival === [[File:小室浅間神社（下宮）神馬舎.jpg|thumb|200px|Shinmesha and the Shinme kept in it]] [[File:Fujiyosida-Yabusame-FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengen.webm|thumb|Yabusame at Fuji San Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine, taken on September 19, 2020]] The Yabusame festival, designated as an Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Yamanashi Prefecture, is held on September 19, the day of the {{ill|Reisai|ja|festival}}, and is famous for the "Horse Hoof Divination" (''batei uranai''). Locally known as "Umatobakashi" (甲州弁: to run the horse), the Yabusame festival is said to have started with a mid-period horseback riding in Chōkan 2 (1164), with the formal Yabusame festival beginning in Angen 2 (1176). The formal practices of the festival, including Asauma (morning horse) and Yuuma (evening horse), were established in Kenkyū 3 (1192), and the festival date was set to September 19 in Eikyō 12 (1440). In the shrine grounds, the sacred horses used for Yabusame are kept. These horses are donated by the Japan Racing Association. This festival is unique from the generally known Yabusame, being closely tied to agricultural faith and the lives of local residents. It features divination by "Ura-bito" (diviners) who interpret the horse hoof prints (batei uranai), oracles (mikuji) to seek divine will, and a week-long purification ritual called "kiribi." The horses for Yabusame are donated by parishioners, and the festival begins with the application and selection of the horses, known as "Uma-dashi no Kushi-uranai," held on January 15, the day after the Tsutsukayū festival. The festival includes the "Hatsu-ma-zoroi" on September 1, "Naka-ma-zoroi" on September 9, "Kessai-hajime" on September 13, "Ato-ma-zoroi" on September 15, "Tenjinsha-sankō and Tenjinsha Sannō-sai" on September 18, the "Reitaisai Yabusame Matsuri" on September 19, and the "Ato-matsuri" on September 20. In the past, families without horses would borrow them from local or neighboring farmers. However, with the decline in horse ownership, the shrine now keeps horses for the festival. Originally held at the "Rokubanba near Nakano Chaya," halfway between the Mount Fuji climbing gate and Umagaeshi, the festival has been performed at the "Honmachi Nakamu Ra Horse Grounds" since the late Edo period. The current horse grounds were used by 1848, as shown in the "festival map of September 19" from that year. [[File:富士山神輿.JPG|200px|thumb|right|Fuji Mountain Mikoshi]] In 2007, after a hiatus, the Fuji Mountain Mikoshi was revived, and its procession takes place on the eve of the festival, September 18. ; Uma-dashi no Kushi-uranai (Horse Selection Divination) : Early morning on January 15, after the results of the Tsutsukayū festival divination are announced, the application for Yabusame horses begins. The horse owners and horses are selected through a divination ritual held at noon. Traditionally, 30 to 60 applications were made for the six horses, and being selected as a horse owner was a great honor. Recently, the number of applications has been lower than the required number. ; Hatsu-ma-zoroi (First Horse Gathering) : On September 1, all horses for the festival gather at the shrine, where a ritual is performed. Each horse owner draws a lot for the practice saddle and receives a set of practice horse gear from the diviners. The horses are then shown to the public and trained (currently, the sacred horses kept at the shrine practice in the shrine grounds). ; Naka-ma-zoroi (Middle Horse Gathering) : On September 9, the horses gather again for a ritual and practice runs. ; Kessai-hajime (Start of Purification) : On September 13, a ritual is held where the scroll with the image of Konohanasakuya-hime and sacred branches are bestowed. The horse owners and participants then enter a purification period and stay in the shrine's purification hall. Previously, this was done at each horse owner's home, where the family, except for the participants, would leave, and a temporary altar was set up for a period of purification. ; Ato-ma-zoroi (Final Horse Gathering) : On September 15, the horses are adorned with decorations, and the participants draw lots for the actual saddle. The diviners then bestow the necessary horse gear for the festival. ; Sannō-sha Yoimiya-sai (Sannō Shrine festival Eve) : On September 17, the participants visit Sannō Shrine for the bow-taking ceremony, where they receive instructions from the diviners. ; Sannō-sha-sai & Yabusame Matsuri Yoimiya-sai (Sannō Shrine festival & Yabusame festival Eve) : On September 18, the priests, diviners, horse owners, and related participants form a procession to Sannō Shrine, and the Fuji Mountain Mikoshi is carried. : That night, a lottery is held to determine the roles of the horses and the order of their runs for the festival the next day. : The horse gear is managed by the "Ura-bito" (diviners), and the decorative "Otenkō" placed on the horse's forehead is woven from the horse's mane and is believed to be a continuation of the horn-shaped decorations seen on horse-shaped haniwa. [[File:馬蹄占流鏑馬.jpg|thumb|278x278px|Yūma running. The horn-shaped decoration on the horse's forehead is called "Otenkō"]] ; Reitaisai Yabusame Matsuri (festival Yabusame festival) : On September 19, arrows, bows, and targets are given to the horse owners, and the Yabusame is performed in the order of Asauma (morning horse) and Yūma (evening horse), followed by the hoof print divination (batei uranai). The festival concludes with the "San'nō-san's Noppalai" (San'nō's farewell run), where the mountain deity is sent back to the mountain after overseeing the autumn harvest. ; Yabusame Ato-matsuri (Yabusame After festival) : On September 20, the results of the hoof print divination are announced and promptly conveyed to each town. ; Ohimaichi : After the Yabusame festival, the priests visit each town for the "Ohimaichi" ritual based on the divination results. : The ritual is held in various locations, from small gatherings of nearby households to larger events at dining halls or community centers. An altar is set up with the deity's scroll, and participants share food and drink. : In each household, a paper talisman from the priest is received to ensure a year free from fires and disputes. === Tsutsukayū festival === [[File:FujisanSimomiyaOmuroSengenShrine Kayu-ura Ritual.jpg|thumb|Tsutsukayū festival conducted overnight by the hereditary diviner family ({{ill|Yoshi no Ike Onsen|ja|葭之池温泉}})]] In Yamanashi Prefecture, the Tsutsukayū festival is held at various shrines in the Fuji Hokuroku and Yatsugatake regions. At Komuro Sengen Shrine, the Tsutsukayū festival is held overnight from January 14 to early morning January 15. The ritual predicts the year's harvest, weather, sericulture, and the number of Fuji pilgrims, with a notable focus on the latterKatsumata (2007), p.643. The results are published as the Tsutsukayū Divination Mark. After the Tsutsukayū ritual, another divination known as "Terifuri Divination" is performed, where a "Katsunoki" (Nured) piece is placed on the embers and its burning pattern is observed to predict the weather. These results are also published. The Tsutsukayū ritual has been documented in the Sengoku-era diary "Katsuyama-ki" as "Tsutsukai," showing that it has remained largely unchanged since thenKatsumata (2007), p.644. The Tsutsukayū ritual is performed by a hereditary diviner family ({{ill|Yoshi no Ike Onsen|ja|葭之池温泉}}). === Okoe-sai (Changing of the deity's Garments) === Every 60 years, the "Okoe-sai" is held to change the garments of the deity (Konohanasakuya-hime). In the 20th century, this ritual was held in 1950 (Shōwa 25). In the Heisei era, it was held on September 19, 2010 (Heisei 22), and the next ritual is scheduled for 2070. It is believed that seeing the deity outside of this ritual brings misfortune. === Shinmeisai (Sacred Horse festival) === Held annually on Children's Day, May 5, it is known as the "festival of Horses and Children." The festival includes gratitude and memorial services for working horses and past sacred horses, and it features stalls and events from local businesses. == Sacred Horses == [[File:冨士山下宮小室浅間神社 JRA奉納 神馬 瑞桜（ヒカリシャーク）.jpg|thumb|Sacred horse 瑞桜 (Hikari Shark)]] Since 1993, sacred horses have been kept at the shrine to maintain and preserve the Yabusame festival and the hoof print divination ritual. {| class="wikitable" |+History of Sacred Horses ! No. ! Horse name ! Sacred Horse name ! Notes |- | 1 | Hikari Shark | 瑞桜 (Zuio) | |- | 2 | Maxport | | |- | 3 | Towa Takeshiba | | |- | 4 | Daiichi Hijiri | | |- | 5 | Tokin | | |- | 6 | Ichiei Clipper | | |- | 7 | Shiro | | |- | 8 | Kings of the Sun | 旺輝 (Ōki) | |- | 9 | Wise Selection | 賢旺 (Kenō) | Current |} The sacred horses, after their lifetime service, are enshrined in the sacred horse shrine. Every year on May 5, the Shinmeisai is held. In addition to the sacred horses, the shrine also keeps Kiso horses and ponies. == Sessha and Massha == === Daitōmiya Shrine and Hinazuru Shrine === * Deities: {{ill|Prince Moriyoshi|ja|護良親王}} and {{ill|Princess Hinazuru|ja|雛鶴姫}} * festival: May 10 (Katsura festival) [[File:Ootounomiya-katura1.jpg|thumb|216px|Sacred Katsura Tree beside the main shrine, known as the "Daitōmiya Katsura Shrine"]] In the shrine grounds, the sacred Katsura tree, known as "Daitōmiya Katsura Shrine," is revered as a deity. According to ancient documents, in the turmoil of the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, the severed head of {{ill|Prince Moriyoshi|ja|護良親王}} was buried at the root of the sacred Katsura tree by Princess Hinazuru. One such document is a copy of a petition dated September 23, Kenmu 2 (1355), from a descendant of Emperor Seiwa. It describes the burial of Prince Moriyoshi's head at the root of the sacred Katsura tree in the shrine grounds and requests that an image of {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshimitsu|ja|源義光}} be carved and secretly worshipped as Prince Moriyoshi alongside the tree. [[File:Ootounomiya-katura2.jpg|thumb|From right to left: Hinazuru Shrine, Daitōmiya Shrine, Head Mound]] The sacred Katsura tree, estimated to be about 800 years old, is designated a natural monument of Fujiyoshida City. === Shinme Shrine === * deity: White Horse Spirit * festival: May 5 (Shinmeisai) The shrine is dedicated to the sacred horse and the spirits of past horses. The Shinmeisai held on May 5 is known as the "festival of Horses," featuring stalls from local businesses and horse riding experiences for children. === Hie Shrine === * deity: {{ill|Ōyamakui|ja|大山咋神}} * festival: May 5 Locally known as the "Monkey Shrine," the shrine features statues of monkeys, which are believed to be divine messengers. === Gosha Shrine (Daishin Shrine, Yama Shrine, Tennō Shrine, Inari Shrine, Tenjin Shrine) === * Deities: Amaterasu Ōmikami, Ōyamatsumi, Susanoo-no-Mikoto, Ōkuninushi, Sukunabikona, Ukanomitama, Sugawara no Michizane * festival: April 10 The shrine combines five shrines into one. === Ebisu Shrine === * deity: {{ill|Ebisu (mythology)|ja|えびす}} * festival: November 19 (Ebisu-kō) The shrine features an Ebisu statue in the style of Ogata Kōrin. The Ebisu-kō festival is held on November 19. === Benzaiten Shrine === * deity: {{ill|Benzaiten|ja|弁才天}} An ancient shrine utilizing a lava tree mold, preserving an old form of Mount Fuji worship. Surrounded by Maruishi stones. === Arata Hachiman Shrine === * Deities: {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ja|応神天皇}}, {{ill|Tama Yorihime|ja|タマヨリビメ (日向神話)}}, {{ill|Empress Jingū|ja|神功皇后}}, Tanabe Ichike ancestor spirits === Suitengu Shrine === * Deities: Amenominakanushi, Emperor Antoku, Takakura Hirashin no Miya (Kenreimon-in, {{ill|Taira no Tokiko|ja|平徳子}}), Nii no Ama ({{ill|Taira no Tokiko|ja|平時子}}) File:Fuji-omurosengen-horse.jpg|Shinme Shrine, sacred horse statue File:Fuji-omurosengen-monkey.jpg|Hie Shrine "See no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil" statues File:FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengenJinja Benten.jpg|Benzaiten Shrine and Maruishi stones File:FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengenJinja ebisu.jpg|Ebisu Shrine File:FujisanSimomiya OmurosengenJinja Gosya.jpg|Gosha Shrine, five-bay structure, remodeled in the Shōwa era File:FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengenJinja suitengu.jpg|Suitengu Shrine File:FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengenJinja aratahatimangu2.jpg|Arata Hachiman Shrine Haiden File:FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengenJinja aratahatimangu.jpg|Arata Hachiman Shrine Honden File:FujisanSimomiya OmuroSengenjinja Gaku.jpg|Great Torii plaque, calligraphy by {{ill|Tokugawa Munetaka|ja|徳川宗敬}}, 1981 (Shōwa 56) File:FujisanSimomiya OmurosengenJinja torii.jpg|Great Torii, completed in 1981 (Shōwa 56), collapsed in 2004 (Heisei 16) due to a typhoon, rebuilt using original materials in 2010 (Heisei 22), with the pillars replaced with steel in 2020 (Reiwa 2) due to severe damage File:Fujisan Simomiya OmuroSengen Jinja Gaku Sindaisugi.jpg|Shindai-sugi plaque in the Haiden, made from a fragment of a sacred ancient cedar struck by lightning in Tenbun and Kan'ei eras, preserved as recorded in Kai Kokushi File:FujisanSimomiyaOmuroSengenJinja Temizu.jpg|Temizuya, built in 1933 (Shōwa 8) to commemorate the birth of Crown Prince Akihito File:FujisanSimomiyaOmuroSengenJinja KaguraDen.jpg|Kagura-den, built in 1975 (Shōwa 50). A rare stage-style Kagura-den in the area, built to accommodate traditional village Kabuki in place of the district's lack of Kagura File:FujisanSimomiya OmurosengenJinja.jpg|Shrine office, an Edo-period building originally used as a village hall, later moved to the shrine grounds and remodeled into the shrine office. A rotating stage and timber framework remain under the tatami mats in the hall. File:Fuji-omurosengen-pond.jpg|Sacred pond == External Shrines == The Fuji San Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine has two exclave grounds where the Konpira Shrine and Shiroō Shrine are enshrined. === Konpira Shrine === * deity: {{ill|Ōmononushi|ja|大物主}} Located in Shimoyoshida Higashimachi, Fujiyoshida City. This area is known as Furuyoshida Morigumi and is said to be the former site of the Fuji San Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine. During the Sengoku period, there was a purification site for Fuji climbers, where spring water was used for cleansing. A checkpoint was also established here to collect tolls, and it marked the starting point for the Yoshida Route to Mount Fuji, as indicated by the "First Step" stone monument. Gekkōji Temple Aizen and FujisanSimomiya Omurosengen KotohiraShrine.jpg|Konpira Shrine of Fuji San Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine and Aizen Jizō Hall of Gekkō-ji Temple. Their proximity indicates their historical relationship. FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengen KotohiraShrine.jpg|Konpira Shrine Honden Fuji Sekisyo .jpg|Stone monuments, including the "First Step" marker indicating the starting point of the Fuji Yoshida Route, located between Konpira Shrine and Aizen Jizō Hall. === Shiroō Shrine (Shiroō Gongen Shrine) === * Deities: Ōkuninushi, Ōtoshi, Shinatobe Located midway up Otaruyama in Fujiyoshida City. About a 20-minute walk east from {{ill|Arakurayama Sengen Park|ja|新倉山浅間公園}}. The festival is held on August 6, known as the "Bug festival" (虫送り), praying for the expulsion of harmful insects and diseases from the fields and homes of Fujiyoshida. The distributed {{ill|Gohei|ja|御幣}} are placed at the entrances of fields and houses. The name Gongen is a remnant of the syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism. Until the mid-Showa period, many people would climb the mountain holding torches to attend the festival. {{ill|Beppyo Shrine|ja|別表神社}} |established = (伝) {{ill|Daidō|ja|大同 (日本)}} 2 (807) |main hall = |alternative name = Shimomiya-san |札所等 = |festival= Yabusame festival (Horse Hoof Divination Ritual) {{ill|September 19|ja|9月19日}} |festival = Tsutsukayū festival January 14
Shinmeisai May 5 |map = {{location map|Japan Yamanashi|lat_deg=35|lat_min=29|lat_sec=41.3|lon_deg=138|lon_min=48|lon_sec=11.4|label=冨士山下宮小室浅間神社|position=bottom|width=200|float=center|caption=|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=20}} {{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=11|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|coord={{coord|35|29|41.36|N|138|48|11.40|E}}}} }} '''{{illOmuro Sengen Shrine (Yamanashi)|lt=Omuro Sengen Shrine|ja|冨士山下宮小室浅間神社}}''' (冨士山下宮小室浅間神社[[ja:冨士山下宮小室浅間神社]]) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Fujiyoshida|ja|富士吉田市}}, {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|ja|山梨県}}. The former rank under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ja|近代rank制度}} was that of a Gōsha, and it is now designated as a Beppyo Shrine under the jurisdiction of the {{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|ja|神社本庁}}. It is one of the many {{ill|Sengen shrines|ja|浅間神社}} across Japan. The former name was '''Fuji San Shimomiya Sengen Shrine'''慶応四年辰年八月の「富士山下宮社地取調書上帳」. The registered name as a religious corporation is '''Komuro Sengen Shrine''' (おむろせんげんじんじゃ). The shrine is dedicated to the {{ill|Ubusunagami|ja|産土神}} of the Fuji Hokuroku region and the entire {{ill|Fujiyoshida|ja|富士吉田市}}, serving as the {{ill|Sōchinju|ja|総鎮守}} of the three villages of Kamiyoshida, Shimoyoshida, and Matsuyama. {{ill|Shinme|ja|神馬}} are kept at the shrine. Locally, it is also referred to as "Shimomiya-san" or "Shimosengen." == Overview == Throughout the year, divination ('''占い''') and oracles ('''神籤(おみくじ）''') play a significant role in the festivals held at the shrine. This includes the "Horse Hoof Divination Yabusame festival" and the "Tsutsukayū festival," which reflect the ancient Fuji worship deeply rooted in the lives of local residents. According to the {{ill|Kai Kokushi|ja|甲斐国志}}, the shrine is the birthplace deity of Kamiyoshida, Shimoyoshida, and Matsuyama villages. Even as other shrines have increased in the surrounding area, the practice of {{ill|Hatsumiya Mairi|ja|初宮参り}} for newborns remains strong, indicating the deep faith of local residents. == Deities == * {{ill|Konohanasakuya-hime|ja|コノハナノサクヤビメ}} == History == According to the shrine legend, in Enryaku 12 (793), {{ill|Sakanoue no Tamuramaro|ja|坂上田村麻呂}}, during his eastern expedition, prayed for victory while worshipping Mount Fuji from Yoshida. After his victory, in gratitude for the divine favor, he built the shrine in Daidō 2 (807). Early records mention the shrine as "Miya" (宮). Until the detailed village survey book of Hōei 3 (1708), it was recorded as "Sengen Miya." Originally, the settlement of Shimoyoshida was located in present-day Shimoyoshida Higashimachi, where it was enshrined at the current location of the {{ill|Higashimachi Kotohira Shrine|ja|東町金毘羅神社}}. Due to frequent snowmelt damage, the settlement and shrine were relocated to their current location, backed by the Kenmaruo Lava Flow{{Cite book|title=下吉田の民俗|date=1990.3.25|year=1990|publisher=富士吉田市教育委員会}}. In Kenmu 2 (1355) on September 23, the head of {{ill|Prince Moriyoshi|ja|護良親王}}, a descendant of Emperor Seiwa, was buried at the root of a sacred katsura tree, and a petition was left behind. In Tenshō 4 (1576), the towns of both Kamiyoshida and Shimoyoshida were completely burned down during the battle between the {{ill|Hōjō clan|ja|北条氏}} and {{ill|Oyamada clan|ja|小山田氏}} ({{ill|Katsuyama-ki|ja|勝山記}}). During the Edo period, the shrine was also the guardian of the largest temple in the Fuji Hokuroku area, {{ill|Gekko-ji|ja|月江寺}}, and until the Meiji era, recitations by Gekko-ji monks were part of the shrine festivals. In Kan'ei 3 (1626) on April 6, a sacred ancient cedar tree in the shrine grounds was struck by lightning and burned ({{ill|Kai Kokushi|ja|甲斐国志}}). A fragment of this tree is displayed as a plaque in the current haiden. The haiden dates back to the Tenshō era (1573-1593). The honden, built by {{ill|Gunai Daiku Nakama|ja|郡内大工仲間}} master carpenter Kayanuma Yasaburō in Meiwa 4 (1767), is the largest single-bay shrine building in Yamanashi Prefecture. This honden served as a model for subsequent shrine buildings in the area. Although it is not registered as a cultural property, it is significant in its architecture. [[File:Fujisan Simomiya Omurosengen Jinjya 冨士山下宮小室浅間神社 本殿.jpg|thumb|250x250px|Honden. Single-bay Irimoya-zukuri style with Karahafu at the front. It is the largest single-bay honden in Yamanashi Prefecture. The eaves are enclosed with covering walls.]] During the Meiji period, the shrine transferred its parishioner area of Kamiyoshida to the {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongū Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮冨士浅間神社}} and changed its name from "Fuji San Shimomiya Sengen Shrine" to the current "Komuro Sengen Shrine." In line with this change, the enshrined deities were unified from "Sengen Daimyōjin, Amaterasu Ōmikami, Inukai Daimyōjin, Aitaka Daigongen, Shinra Saburō Yoshimitsu (Prince Moriyoshi)" to "Konohanasakuya-hime (Sengen Ōkami)." The shrine crest was also changed from "Shuro no Ha" to "Yamato Yaezakura." Amaterasu Ōmikami was moved to the Gosha Shrine, and Prince Moriyoshi was enshrined separately in the Daitōmiya Shrine. In 1957, the shrine exchanged its grounds and municipal land on Otaruyama with the neighboring Shimoyoshida First Elementary School for playground expansion. In the same year, it was designated a Beppyo Shrine. === Origin of the name "Shimomiya" === The term "Shimomiya" refers to the lower shrine in relation to Mount Fuji, with no specific upper shrine. There are several theories as to why it is called "Shimomiya." # Originally referred to simply as "Miya," it was called "Shimomiya" to distinguish it from other Sengen shrines that began to enshrine Sengen Ōkami in the villages, referring to the shrine lower in relation to Mount Fuji{{Cite web|和書|title=富士山下宮小室浅間神社　由諸|url=http://www.fgo.jp/~yabusame/rekisi.htm|website=www.fgo.jp|accessdate=2019-09-09}}. # The term "Shimomiya" was used by people around Lake Kawaguchi to refer to the Fuji Yoshida area, distinguishing it from {{ill|Kawaguchi Sengen Shrine|ja|河口浅間神社}}. # The term "Shimomiya" referred to the lower shrine in relation to the Komuro Sengen Shrine at the second station of Mount Fuji (now the former main shrine of the {{ill|Fuji Omuro Sengen Shrine|ja|冨士御室浅間神社}}). This theory, however, has been widely spread but is now considered a folk belief, as shown by the following points: #* Both shrines have different origins and histories. #* The {{ill|Kai Kokushi|ja|甲斐国志}} mentions the Komuro Sengen Shrine's satomiya in Katsuyama, but there is no mention of the relationship with Shimomiya Sengen. #* The Komuro Sengen Shrine at the second station was easily acquired by Katsuyama in Fujikawaguchiko as an exclave. #* The shrine building from the second station was moved to the satomiya grounds in Katsuyama. #* The relationship with the Komuro Sengen Shrine at the second station was not proven, so it was excluded from the list of components for the Mount Fuji World Cultural Heritage designation (it was seen more as a birthplace, tutelary, or guardian deity, deeply rooted in local life rather than Fuji worship). #* During the Meiji period, another shrine in the same city, Ōasumi's {{ill|Komuro Sengen Shrine (Fujiyoshida Ōasumi)|ja|小室浅間神社 (富士吉田市大明見)}}, was renamed to "Komuro Sengen Shrine." #* The Yabusame festival was traditionally held together, but the records and descriptions, such as the {{ill|Katsuyama-ki|ja|勝山記}} and {{ill|Myōhō-ji-ki|ja|妙法寺記}}, do not mention horse hoof divination or divination rituals in Katsuyama. #* The place where the Yabusame was held is described as "Rokubanba near Nakano Chaya" in theory 3, but it is actually "Nakano Chaya near the second station," which is far apart, showing no connection between Rokubanba and the Komuro Sengen Shrine at the second station. #* The Yabusame was performed by various shrines and villages in the Fuji Hokuroku area. Over time, the Rokubanba became the Nagabanba, and the ceremonies became more localized. #* As mentioned below, there is confusion between "Shimomiya" and "Shimoyashima." === Confusion between "Shimoyashima" and "Shimomiya" === In {{ill|Fujiyoshida|ja|富士吉田市}}, the {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongū Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮冨士浅間神社}} is located in Kamiyoshida, while the Komuro Sengen Shrine is in Shimoyoshida. Therefore, it is easy to mistake the Komuro Sengen Shrine as the "Shimomiya" in contrast to the "Hongū" of Kitaguchi. In modern times, the Kitaguchi Hongū is referred to as "Kami Sengen" or "Kami Sen," and the Komuro Sengen Shrine as "Shimoyashima" or "Shimo Sen," which further perpetuates the confusion. However, '''"Shimoyashima" originally referred to the {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongū Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮冨士浅間神社}} rather than the Fuji San Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine'''{{Cite web|和書|url=https://www.pref.yamanashi.jp/fujisan/rebirth/documents/fujisanmichi-omote.pdf|title=富士参詣富士山道表|accessdate=2019.02|publisher=山梨県富士山世界文化遺産保存活用推進協議会}}. For example, the 'Hachiyō Kunsun-zu' from Enpō 8 (1680), which depicts the Yoshida Route to Mount Fuji, refers to the current Kitaguchi Hongū grounds as "Shimoyashima"{{Cite journal|author=串田優子 伊藤裕久|year=2006|title=北口本宮冨士浅間神社境内空間の変遷過程|journal=日本建築学会計画系論文集|volume=第604号|page=159−16S}}. Additionally, the 'Kai Kokushi' from Bunka 11 (1814) describes the Komuro Sengen Shrine at the second station (now Fuji Omuro Sengen Shrine) as "Kami Sengen," and the shrine at Kitaguchi as "Shimoyashima," with the shrine at Shimoyoshida referred to as "Shimomiya Sengen." From the above, it is clear that "Shimoyashima" and "Shimomiya Sengen" were separate entities. However, after the transfer of the parishioner area of Kamiyoshida to Kitaguchi Hongū, the relationship with the Komuro Sengen Shrine at the second station in Katsuyama of Fujikawaguchiko weakened. Thus, the term "Kami Sengen" ceased to be used for the second station shrine, leading to the Kitaguchi Hongū being referred to as "Kami Sengen" and the Komuro Sengen Shrine as "Shimoyashima," with the latter being renamed to "Komuro Sengen Shrine" during the Meiji period, further perpetuating the confusion between "Shimoyashima" and "Shimomiya." == festivals == === Yabusame festival === [[File:小室浅間神社（下宮）神馬舎.jpg|thumb|200px|Shinmesha and the Shinme kept in it]] [[File:Fujiyosida-Yabusame-FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengen.webm|thumb|Yabusame at Fuji San Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine, taken on September 19, 2020]] The Yabusame festival, designated as an Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Yamanashi Prefecture, is held on September 19, the day of the {{ill|Reisai|ja|festival}}, and is famous for the "Horse Hoof Divination" (''batei uranai''). Locally known as "Umatobakashi" (甲州弁: to run the horse), the Yabusame festival is said to have started with a mid-period horseback riding in Chōkan 2 (1164), with the formal Yabusame festival beginning in Angen 2 (1176). The formal practices of the festival, including Asauma (morning horse) and Yuuma (evening horse), were established in Kenkyū 3 (1192), and the festival date was set to September 19 in Eikyō 12 (1440). In the shrine grounds, the sacred horses used for Yabusame are kept. These horses are donated by the Japan Racing Association. This festival is unique from the generally known Yabusame, being closely tied to agricultural faith and the lives of local residents. It features divination by "Ura-bito" (diviners) who interpret the horse hoof prints (batei uranai), oracles (mikuji) to seek divine will, and a week-long purification ritual called "kiribi." The horses for Yabusame are donated by parishioners, and the festival begins with the application and selection of the horses, known as "Uma-dashi no Kushi-uranai," held on January 15, the day after the Tsutsukayū festival. The festival includes the "Hatsu-ma-zoroi" on September 1, "Naka-ma-zoroi" on September 9, "Kessai-hajime" on September 13, "Ato-ma-zoroi" on September 15, "Tenjinsha-sankō and Tenjinsha Sannō-sai" on September 18, the "Reitaisai Yabusame Matsuri" on September 19, and the "Ato-matsuri" on September 20. In the past, families without horses would borrow them from local or neighboring farmers. However, with the decline in horse ownership, the shrine now keeps horses for the festival. Originally held at the "Rokubanba near Nakano Chaya," halfway between the Mount Fuji climbing gate and Umagaeshi, the festival has been performed at the "Honmachi Nakamu Ra Horse Grounds" since the late Edo period. The current horse grounds were used by 1848, as shown in the "festival map of September 19" from that year. [[File:富士山神輿.JPG|200px|thumb|right|Fuji Mountain Mikoshi]] In 2007, after a hiatus, the Fuji Mountain Mikoshi was revived, and its procession takes place on the eve of the festival, September 18. ; Uma-dashi no Kushi-uranai (Horse Selection Divination) : Early morning on January 15, after the results of the Tsutsukayū festival divination are announced, the application for Yabusame horses begins. The horse owners and horses are selected through a divination ritual held at noon. Traditionally, 30 to 60 applications were made for the six horses, and being selected as a horse owner was a great honor. Recently, the number of applications has been lower than the required number. ; Hatsu-ma-zoroi (First Horse Gathering) : On September 1, all horses for the festival gather at the shrine, where a ritual is performed. Each horse owner draws a lot for the practice saddle and receives a set of practice horse gear from the diviners. The horses are then shown to the public and trained (currently, the sacred horses kept at the shrine practice in the shrine grounds). ; Naka-ma-zoroi (Middle Horse Gathering) : On September 9, the horses gather again for a ritual and practice runs. ; Kessai-hajime (Start of Purification) : On September 13, a ritual is held where the scroll with the image of Konohanasakuya-hime and sacred branches are bestowed. The horse owners and participants then enter a purification period and stay in the shrine's purification hall. Previously, this was done at each horse owner's home, where the family, except for the participants, would leave, and a temporary altar was set up for a period of purification. ; Ato-ma-zoroi (Final Horse Gathering) : On September 15, the horses are adorned with decorations, and the participants draw lots for the actual saddle. The diviners then bestow the necessary horse gear for the festival. ; Sannō-sha Yoimiya-sai (Sannō Shrine festival Eve) : On September 17, the participants visit Sannō Shrine for the bow-taking ceremony, where they receive instructions from the diviners. ; Sannō-sha-sai & Yabusame Matsuri Yoimiya-sai (Sannō Shrine festival & Yabusame festival Eve) : On September 18, the priests, diviners, horse owners, and related participants form a procession to Sannō Shrine, and the Fuji Mountain Mikoshi is carried. : That night, a lottery is held to determine the roles of the horses and the order of their runs for the festival the next day. : The horse gear is managed by the "Ura-bito" (diviners), and the decorative "Otenkō" placed on the horse's forehead is woven from the horse's mane and is believed to be a continuation of the horn-shaped decorations seen on horse-shaped haniwa. [[File:馬蹄占流鏑馬.jpg|thumb|278x278px|Yūma running. The horn-shaped decoration on the horse's forehead is called "Otenkō"]] ; Reitaisai Yabusame Matsuri (festival Yabusame festival) : On September 19, arrows, bows, and targets are given to the horse owners, and the Yabusame is performed in the order of Asauma (morning horse) and Yūma (evening horse), followed by the hoof print divination (batei uranai). The festival concludes with the "San'nō-san's Noppalai" (San'nō's farewell run), where the mountain deity is sent back to the mountain after overseeing the autumn harvest. ; Yabusame Ato-matsuri (Yabusame After festival) : On September 20, the results of the hoof print divination are announced and promptly conveyed to each town. ; Ohimaichi : After the Yabusame festival, the priests visit each town for the "Ohimaichi" ritual based on the divination results. : The ritual is held in various locations, from small gatherings of nearby households to larger events at dining halls or community centers. An altar is set up with the deity's scroll, and participants share food and drink. : In each household, a paper talisman from the priest is received to ensure a year free from fires and disputes. === Tsutsukayū festival === [[File:FujisanSimomiyaOmuroSengenShrine Kayu-ura Ritual.jpg|thumb|Tsutsukayū festival conducted overnight by the hereditary diviner family ({{ill|Yoshi no Ike Onsen|ja|葭之池温泉}})]] In Yamanashi Prefecture, the Tsutsukayū festival is held at various shrines in the Fuji Hokuroku and Yatsugatake regions. At Komuro Sengen Shrine, the Tsutsukayū festival is held overnight from January 14 to early morning January 15. The ritual predicts the year's harvest, weather, sericulture, and the number of Fuji pilgrims, with a notable focus on the latterKatsumata (2007), p.643. The results are published as the Tsutsukayū Divination Mark. After the Tsutsukayū ritual, another divination known as "Terifuri Divination" is performed, where a "Katsunoki" (Nured) piece is placed on the embers and its burning pattern is observed to predict the weather. These results are also published. The Tsutsukayū ritual has been documented in the Sengoku-era diary "Katsuyama-ki" as "Tsutsukai," showing that it has remained largely unchanged since thenKatsumata (2007), p.644. The Tsutsukayū ritual is performed by a hereditary diviner family ({{ill|Yoshi no Ike Onsen|ja|葭之池温泉}}). === Okoe-sai (Changing of the deity's Garments) === Every 60 years, the "Okoe-sai" is held to change the garments of the deity (Konohanasakuya-hime). In the 20th century, this ritual was held in 1950 (Shōwa 25). In the Heisei era, it was held on September 19, 2010 (Heisei 22), and the next ritual is scheduled for 2070. It is believed that seeing the deity outside of this ritual brings misfortune. === Shinmeisai (Sacred Horse festival) === Held annually on Children's Day, May 5, it is known as the "festival of Horses and Children." The festival includes gratitude and memorial services for working horses and past sacred horses, and it features stalls and events from local businesses. == Sacred Horses == [[File:冨士山下宮小室浅間神社 JRA奉納 神馬 瑞桜（ヒカリシャーク）.jpg|thumb|Sacred horse 瑞桜 (Hikari Shark)]] Since 1993, sacred horses have been kept at the shrine to maintain and preserve the Yabusame festival and the hoof print divination ritual. {| class="wikitable" |+History of Sacred Horses ! No. ! Horse name ! Sacred Horse name ! Notes |- | 1 | Hikari Shark | 瑞桜 (Zuio) | |- | 2 | Maxport | | |- | 3 | Towa Takeshiba | | |- | 4 | Daiichi Hijiri | | |- | 5 | Tokin | | |- | 6 | Ichiei Clipper | | |- | 7 | Shiro | | |- | 8 | Kings of the Sun | 旺輝 (Ōki) | |- | 9 | Wise Selection | 賢旺 (Kenō) | Current |} The sacred horses, after their lifetime service, are enshrined in the sacred horse shrine. Every year on May 5, the Shinmeisai is held. In addition to the sacred horses, the shrine also keeps Kiso horses and ponies. == Sessha and Massha == === Daitōmiya Shrine and Hinazuru Shrine === * Deities: {{ill|Prince Moriyoshi|ja|護良親王}} and {{ill|Princess Hinazuru|ja|雛鶴姫}} * festival: May 10 (Katsura festival) [[File:Ootounomiya-katura1.jpg|thumb|216px|Sacred Katsura Tree beside the main shrine, known as the "Daitōmiya Katsura Shrine"]] In the shrine grounds, the sacred Katsura tree, known as "Daitōmiya Katsura Shrine," is revered as a deity. According to ancient documents, in the turmoil of the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, the severed head of {{ill|Prince Moriyoshi|ja|護良親王}} was buried at the root of the sacred Katsura tree by Princess Hinazuru. One such document is a copy of a petition dated September 23, Kenmu 2 (1355), from a descendant of Emperor Seiwa. It describes the burial of Prince Moriyoshi's head at the root of the sacred Katsura tree in the shrine grounds and requests that an image of {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshimitsu|ja|源義光}} be carved and secretly worshipped as Prince Moriyoshi alongside the tree. [[File:Ootounomiya-katura2.jpg|thumb|From right to left: Hinazuru Shrine, Daitōmiya Shrine, Head Mound]] The sacred Katsura tree, estimated to be about 800 years old, is designated a natural monument of Fujiyoshida City. === Shinme Shrine === * deity: White Horse Spirit * festival: May 5 (Shinmeisai) The shrine is dedicated to the sacred horse and the spirits of past horses. The Shinmeisai held on May 5 is known as the "festival of Horses," featuring stalls from local businesses and horse riding experiences for children. === Hie Shrine === * deity: {{ill|Ōyamakui|ja|大山咋神}} * festival: May 5 Locally known as the "Monkey Shrine," the shrine features statues of monkeys, which are believed to be divine messengers. === Gosha Shrine (Daishin Shrine, Yama Shrine, Tennō Shrine, Inari Shrine, Tenjin Shrine) === * Deities: Amaterasu Ōmikami, Ōyamatsumi, Susanoo-no-Mikoto, Ōkuninushi, Sukunabikona, Ukanomitama, Sugawara no Michizane * festival: April 10 The shrine combines five shrines into one. === Ebisu Shrine === * deity: {{ill|Ebisu (mythology)|ja|えびす}} * festival: November 19 (Ebisu-kō) The shrine features an Ebisu statue in the style of Ogata Kōrin. The Ebisu-kō festival is held on November 19. === Benzaiten Shrine === * deity: {{ill|Benzaiten|ja|弁才天}} An ancient shrine utilizing a lava tree mold, preserving an old form of Mount Fuji worship. Surrounded by Maruishi stones. === Arata Hachiman Shrine === * Deities: {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ja|応神天皇}}, {{ill|Tama Yorihime|ja|タマヨリビメ (日向神話)}}, {{ill|Empress Jingū|ja|神功皇后}}, Tanabe Ichike ancestor spirits === Suitengu Shrine === * Deities: Amenominakanushi, Emperor Antoku, Takakura Hirashin no Miya (Kenreimon-in, {{ill|Taira no Tokiko|ja|平徳子}}), Nii no Ama ({{ill|Taira no Tokiko|ja|平時子}}) File:Fuji-omurosengen-horse.jpg|Shinme Shrine, sacred horse statue File:Fuji-omurosengen-monkey.jpg|Hie Shrine "See no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil" statues File:FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengenJinja Benten.jpg|Benzaiten Shrine and Maruishi stones File:FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengenJinja ebisu.jpg|Ebisu Shrine File:FujisanSimomiya OmurosengenJinja Gosya.jpg|Gosha Shrine, five-bay structure, remodeled in the Shōwa era File:FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengenJinja suitengu.jpg|Suitengu Shrine File:FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengenJinja aratahatimangu2.jpg|Arata Hachiman Shrine Haiden File:FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengenJinja aratahatimangu.jpg|Arata Hachiman Shrine Honden File:FujisanSimomiya OmuroSengenjinja Gaku.jpg|Great Torii plaque, calligraphy by {{ill|Tokugawa Munetaka|ja|徳川宗敬}}, 1981 (Shōwa 56) File:FujisanSimomiya OmurosengenJinja torii.jpg|Great Torii, completed in 1981 (Shōwa 56), collapsed in 2004 (Heisei 16) due to a typhoon, rebuilt using original materials in 2010 (Heisei 22), with the pillars replaced with steel in 2020 (Reiwa 2) due to severe damage File:Fujisan Simomiya OmuroSengen Jinja Gaku Sindaisugi.jpg|Shindai-sugi plaque in the Haiden, made from a fragment of a sacred ancient cedar struck by lightning in Tenbun and Kan'ei eras, preserved as recorded in Kai Kokushi File:FujisanSimomiyaOmuroSengenJinja Temizu.jpg|Temizuya, built in 1933 (Shōwa 8) to commemorate the birth of Crown Prince Akihito File:FujisanSimomiyaOmuroSengenJinja KaguraDen.jpg|Kagura-den, built in 1975 (Shōwa 50). A rare stage-style Kagura-den in the area, built to accommodate traditional village Kabuki in place of the district's lack of Kagura File:FujisanSimomiya OmurosengenJinja.jpg|Shrine office, an Edo-period building originally used as a village hall, later moved to the shrine grounds and remodeled into the shrine office. A rotating stage and timber framework remain under the tatami mats in the hall. File:Fuji-omurosengen-pond.jpg|Sacred pond == External Shrines == The Fuji San Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine has two exclave grounds where the Konpira Shrine and Shiroō Shrine are enshrined. === Konpira Shrine === * deity: {{ill|Ōmononushi|ja|大物主}} Located in Shimoyoshida Higashimachi, Fujiyoshida City. This area is known as Furuyoshida Morigumi and is said to be the former site of the Fuji San Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine. During the Sengoku period, there was a purification site for Fuji climbers, where spring water was used for cleansing. A checkpoint was also established here to collect tolls, and it marked the starting point for the Yoshida Route to Mount Fuji, as indicated by the "First Step" stone monument. Gekkōji Temple Aizen and FujisanSimomiya Omurosengen KotohiraShrine.jpg|Konpira Shrine of Fuji San Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine and Aizen Jizō Hall of Gekkō-ji Temple. Their proximity indicates their historical relationship. FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengen KotohiraShrine.jpg|Konpira Shrine Honden Fuji Sekisyo .jpg|Stone monuments, including the "First Step" marker indicating the starting point of the Fuji Yoshida Route, located between Konpira Shrine and Aizen Jizō Hall. === Shiroō Shrine (Shiroō Gongen Shrine) === * Deities: Ōkuninushi, Ōtoshi, Shinatobe Located midway up Otaruyama in Fujiyoshida City. About a 20-minute walk east from {{ill|Arakurayama Sengen Park|ja|新倉山浅間公園}}. The festival is held on August 6, known as the "Bug festival" (虫送り), praying for the expulsion of harmful insects and diseases from the fields and homes of Fujiyoshida. The distributed {{ill|Gohei|ja|御幣}} are placed at the entrances of fields and houses. The name Gongen is a remnant of the syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism. Until the mid-Showa period, many people would climb the mountain holding torches to attend the festival.
