Torii and Haiden |location = {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|ja|山梨県}} {{ill|Fujiyoshida|ja|富士吉田市}} Shimoyoshida 3-32-18 |coordinates = {{coord|35|29|41.36|N|138|48|11.40|E|region:JP-19_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Komuro Sengen Shrine}} |deity = {{ill|Konohanasakuya-hime|ja|コノハナノサクヤビメ}} |神体 = Mount Fuji |Rank = Former {{ill|Gōsha|ja|近代Rank制度#諸社}}
{{ill|Beppyo Shrine|ja|別表神社}} |established = (伝) {{ill|Daidō|ja|大同 (日本)}} 2 (807) |main hall = |alternative name = Shimomiya-san |札所等 = |festival= Yabusame festival (Horse Hoof Divination Ritual) {{ill|September 19|ja|9月19日}} |festival = Tsutsukayū festival January 14
Shinmeisai May 5 |map = {{location map|Japan Yamanashi|lat_deg=35|lat_min=29|lat_sec=41.3|lon_deg=138|lon_min=48|lon_sec=11.4|label=冨士山下宮小室浅間神社|position=bottom|width=200|float=center|caption=|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=20}} {{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=11|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|coord={{coord|35|29|41.36|N|138|48|11.40|E}}}} }} '''{{ill|Omuro Sengen Shrine (Yamanashi)|lt=Omuro Sengen Shrine|ja|冨士山下宮小室浅間神社}}''' (冨士山下宮小室浅間神社) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Fujiyoshida|ja|富士吉田市}}, {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|ja|山梨県}}. The former Rank under the {{ill|Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|ja|近代Rank制度}} was that of a Gōsha, and it is now designated as a Beppyo Shrine under the jurisdiction of the {{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|ja|神社本庁}}. It is one of the many {{ill|Sengen shrines|ja|浅間神社}} across Japan. The former name was '''Fuji San Shimomiya Sengen Shrine'''慶応四年辰年八月の「富士山下宮社地取調書上帳」. The shrine is dedicated to the {{ill|Ubusunagami|ja|産土神|1=Ubusunagami}} of the Fuji Hokuroku region and the entire {{ill|Fujiyoshida|ja|富士吉田市}}, serving as the {{ill|Chinjugami|ja|総鎮守}} of the three villages of Kamiyoshida, Shimoyoshida, and Matsuyama. {{ill|Shinme|ja|神馬}} are kept at the shrine. Locally, it is also referred to as "Shimomiya-san" or "Shimosengen." == Overview == Throughout the year, divination ('''占い''') and oracles ('''神籤(おみくじ）''') play a significant role in the festivals held at the shrine. This includes the "Horse Hoof Divination Yabusame festival" and the "Tsutsukayū festival," which reflect the ancient Fuji worship deeply rooted in the lives of local residents. According to the {{ill|Kai Kokushi|ja|甲斐国志}}, the shrine is the birthplace deity of Kamiyoshida, Shimoyoshida, and Matsuyama villages. Even as other shrines have increased in the surrounding area, the practice of {{ill|Hatsumiya Mairi|ja|初宮参り}} for newborns remains strong, indicating the deep faith of local residents. == Deities == * {{ill|Konohanasakuya-hime|ja|コノハナノサクヤビメ}} == History == According to the shrine legend, in Enryaku 12 (793), {{ill|Sakanoue no Tamuramaro|ja|坂上田村麻呂}}, during his eastern expedition, prayed for victory while worshipping Mount Fuji from Yoshida. After his victory, in gratitude for the divine favor, he built the shrine in Daidō 2 (807). Early records mention the shrine as "Miya" (宮). Until the detailed village survey book of Hōei 3 (1708), it was recorded as "Sengen Miya." Originally, the settlement of Shimoyoshida was located in present-day Shimoyoshida Higashimachi, where it was enshrined at the current location of the {{ill|Higashimachi Kotohira Shrine|ja|東町金毘羅神社}}. Due to frequent snowmelt damage, the settlement and shrine were relocated to their current location, backed by the Kenmaruo Lava Flow{{Cite book|title=下吉田の民俗|date=1990.3.25|year=1990|publisher=富士吉田市教育委員会}}. In Kenmu 2 (1355) on September 23, the head of {{ill|Prince Moriyoshi|ja|護良親王}}, a descendant of Emperor Seiwa, was buried at the root of a sacred katsura tree, and a petition was left behind. In Tenshō 4 (1576), the towns of both Kamiyoshida and Shimoyoshida were completely burned down during the battle between the {{ill|Hōjō clan|ja|北条氏}} and {{ill|Oyamada clan|ja|小山田氏}} ({{ill|Katsuyama-ki|ja|勝山記}}). During the Edo period, the shrine was also the guardian of the largest temple in the Fuji Hokuroku area, {{ill|Gekko-ji|ja|月江寺}}, and until the Meiji era, recitations by Gekko-ji monks were part of the shrine festivals. In Kan'ei 3 (1626) on April 6, a sacred ancient cedar tree in the shrine grounds was struck by lightning and burned ({{ill|Kai Kokushi|ja|甲斐国志}}). A fragment of this tree is displayed as a plaque in the current haiden. The haiden dates back to the Tenshō era (1573-1593). The honden, built by {{ill|Gunai Daiku Nakama|ja|郡内大工仲間}} master carpenter Kayanuma Yasaburō in Meiwa 4 (1767), is the largest single-bay shrine building in Yamanashi Prefecture. This honden served as a model for subsequent shrine buildings in the area. Although it is not registered as a cultural property, it is significant in its architecture. [[File:Fujisan Simomiya Omurosengen Jinjya 冨士山下宮小室浅間神社 本殿.jpg|thumb|250x250px|Honden. Single-bay Irimoya-zukuri style with Karahafu at the front. It is the largest single-bay honden in Yamanashi Prefecture. The eaves are enclosed with covering walls.]] During the Meiji period, the shrine transferred its parishioner area of Kamiyoshida to the {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongū Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮冨士浅間神社}} and changed its name from "Fuji San Shimomiya Sengen Shrine" to the current "Komuro Sengen Shrine." In line with this change, the enshrined deities were unified from "Sengen Daimyōjin, Amaterasu Ōmikami, Inukai Daimyōjin, Aitaka Daigongen, Shinra Saburō Yoshimitsu (Prince Moriyoshi)" to "Konohanasakuya-hime (Sengen Ōkami)." The shrine crest was also changed from "Shuro no Ha" to "Yamato Yaezakura." Amaterasu Ōmikami was moved to the Gosha Shrine, and Prince Moriyoshi was enshrined separately in the Daitōmiya Shrine. In 1957, the shrine exchanged its grounds and municipal land on Otaruyama with the neighboring Shimoyoshida First Elementary School for playground expansion. In the same year, it was designated a Beppyo Shrine. === Origin of the name "Shimomiya" === The term "Shimomiya" refers to the lower shrine in relation to Mount Fuji, with no specific upper shrine. There are several theories as to why it is called "Shimomiya." # Originally referred to simply as "Miya," it was called "Shimomiya" to distinguish it from other Sengen shrines that began to enshrine Sengen Ōkami in the villages, referring to the shrine lower in relation to Mount Fuji{{Cite web|和書|title=富士山下宮小室浅間神社　由諸|url=http://www.fgo.jp/~yabusame/rekisi.htm|website=www.fgo.jp|accessdate=2019-09-09}}. # The term "Shimomiya" was used by people around Lake Kawaguchi to refer to the Fuji Yoshida area, distinguishing it from {{ill|Kawaguchi Sengen Shrine|ja|河口浅間神社}}. # The term "Shimomiya" referred to the lower shrine in relation to the Komuro Sengen Shrine at the second station of Mount Fuji (now the former main shrine of the {{ill|Fuji Omuro Sengen Shrine|ja|冨士御室浅間神社}}). This theory, however, has been widely spread but is now considered a folk belief, as shown by the following points: #* Both shrines have different origins and histories. #* The {{ill|Kai Kokushi|ja|甲斐国志}} mentions the Komuro Sengen Shrine's satomiya in Katsuyama, but there is no mention of the relationship with Shimomiya Sengen. #* The Komuro Sengen Shrine at the second station was easily acquired by Katsuyama in Fujikawaguchiko as an exclave. #* The shrine building from the second station was moved to the satomiya grounds in Katsuyama. #* The relationship with the Komuro Sengen Shrine at the second station was not proven, so it was excluded from the list of components for the Mount Fuji World Cultural Heritage designation (it was seen more as a birthplace, tutelary, or guardian deity, deeply rooted in local life rather than Fuji worship). #* During the Meiji period, another shrine in the same city, Ōasumi's {{ill|Komuro Sengen Shrine (Fujiyoshida Ōasumi)|ja|小室浅間神社 (富士吉田市大明見)}}, was renamed to "Komuro Sengen Shrine." #* The Yabusame festival was traditionally held together, but the records and descriptions, such as the {{ill|Katsuyama-ki|ja|勝山記}} and {{ill|Myōhō-ji-ki|ja|妙法寺記}}, do not mention horse hoof divination or divination rituals in Katsuyama. #* The place where the Yabusame was held is described as "Rokubanba near Nakano Chaya" in theory 3, but it is actually "Nakano Chaya near the second station," which is far apart, showing no connection between Rokubanba and the Komuro Sengen Shrine at the second station. #* The Yabusame was performed by various shrines and villages in the Fuji Hokuroku area. Over time, the Rokubanba became the Nagabanba, and the ceremonies became more localized. #* As mentioned below, there is confusion between "Shimomiya" and "Shimoyashima." === Confusion between "Shimoyashima" and "Shimomiya" === In {{ill|Fujiyoshida|ja|富士吉田市}}, the {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongū Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮冨士浅間神社}} is located in Kamiyoshida, while the Komuro Sengen Shrine is in Shimoyoshida. Therefore, it is easy to mistake the Komuro Sengen Shrine as the "Shimomiya" in contrast to the "Hongū" of Kitaguchi. In modern times, the Kitaguchi Hongū is referred to as "Kami Sengen" or "Kami Sen," and the Komuro Sengen Shrine as "Shimoyashima" or "Shimo Sen," which further perpetuates the confusion. However, '''"Shimoyashima" originally referred to the {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongū Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮冨士浅間神社}} rather than the Fuji San Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine'''{{Cite web|和書|url=https://www.pref.yamanashi.jp/fujisan/rebirth/documents/fujisanmichi-omote.pdf|title=富士参詣富士山道表|accessdate=2019.02|publisher=山梨県富士山世界文化遺産保存活用推進協議会}}. For example, the 'Hachiyō Kunsun-zu' from Enpō 8 (1680), which depicts the Yoshida Route to Mount Fuji, refers to the current Kitaguchi Hongū grounds as "Shimoyashima"{{Cite journal|author=串田優子 伊藤裕久|year=2006|title=北口本宮冨士浅間神社境内空間の変遷過程|journal=日本建築学会計画系論文集|volume=第604号|page=159−16S}}. Additionally, the 'Kai Kokushi' from Bunka 11 (1814) describes the Komuro Sengen Shrine at the second station (now Fuji Omuro Sengen Shrine) as "Kami Sengen," and the shrine at Kitaguchi as "Shimoyashima," with the shrine at Shimoyoshida referred to as "Shimomiya Sengen." From the above, it is clear that "Shimoyashima" and "Shimomiya Sengen" were separate entities. However, after the transfer of the parishioner area of Kamiyoshida to Kitaguchi Hongū, the relationship with the Komuro Sengen Shrine at the second station in Katsuyama of Fujikawaguchiko weakened. Thus, the term "Kami Sengen" ceased to be used for the second station shrine, leading to the Kitaguchi Hongū being referred to as "Kami Sengen" and the Komuro Sengen Shrine as "Shimoyashima," with the latter being renamed to "Komuro Sengen Shrine" during the Meiji period, further perpetuating the confusion between "Shimoyashima" and "Shimomiya." == festivals == === Yabusame festival === [[File:小室浅間神社（下宮）神馬舎.jpg|thumb|200px|Shinmesha and the Shinme kept in it]] [[File:Fujiyosida-Yabusame-FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengen.webm|thumb|Yabusame at Fuji San Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine, taken on September 19, 2020]] The Yabusame festival, designated as an Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Yamanashi Prefecture, is held on September 19, the day of the {{ill|Reisai|ja|festival}}, and is famous for the "Horse Hoof Divination" (''batei uranai''). Locally known as "Umatobakashi" (甲州弁: to run the horse), the Yabusame festival is said to have started with a mid-period horseback riding in Chōkan 2 (1164), with the formal Yabusame festival beginning in Angen 2 (1176). The formal practices of the festival, including Asauma (morning horse) and Yuuma (evening horse), were established in Kenkyū 3 (1192), and the festival date was set to September 19 in Eikyō 12 (1440). In the shrine grounds, the sacred horses used for Yabusame are kept. These horses are donated by the Japan Racing Association. This festival is unique from the generally known Yabusame, being closely tied to agricultural faith and the lives of local residents. It features divination by "Ura-bito" (diviners) who interpret the horse hoof prints (batei uranai), oracles (mikuji) to seek divine will, and a week-long purification ritual called "kiribi." The horses for Yabusame are donated by parishioners, and the festival begins with the application and selection of the horses, known as "Uma-dashi no Kushi-uranai," held on January 15, the day after the Tsutsukayū festival. The festival includes the "Hatsu-ma-zoroi" on September 1, "Naka-ma-zoroi" on September 9, "Kessai-hajime" on September 13, "Ato-ma-zoroi" on September 15, "Tenjinsha-sankō and Tenjinsha Sannō-sai" on September 18, the "Reitaisai Yabusame Matsuri" on September 19, and the "Ato-matsuri" on September 20. In the past, families without horses would borrow them from local or neighboring farmers. However, with the decline in horse ownership, the shrine now keeps horses for the festival. Originally held at the "Rokubanba near Nakano Chaya," halfway between the Mount Fuji climbing gate and Umagaeshi, the festival has been performed at the "Honmachi Nakamu Ra Horse Grounds" since the late Edo period. The current horse grounds were used by 1848, as shown in the "festival map of September 19" from that year. [[File:富士山神輿.JPG|200px|thumb|right|Fuji Mountain Mikoshi]] In 2007, after a hiatus, the Fuji Mountain Mikoshi was revived, and its procession takes place on the eve of the festival, September 18. ; Uma-dashi no Kushi-uranai (Horse Selection Divination) : Early morning on January 15, after the results of the Tsutsukayū festival divination are announced, the application for Yabusame horses begins. The horse owners and horses are selected through a divination ritual held at noon. Traditionally, 30 to 60 applications were made for the six horses, and being selected as a horse owner was a great honor. Recently, the number of applications has been lower than the required number. ; Hatsu-ma-zoroi (First Horse Gathering) : On September 1, all horses for the festival gather at the shrine, where a ritual is performed. Each horse owner draws a lot for the practice saddle and receives a set of practice horse gear from the diviners. The horses are then shown to the public and trained (currently, the sacred horses kept at the shrine practice in the shrine grounds). ; Naka-ma-zoroi (Middle Horse Gathering) : On September 9, the horses gather again for a ritual and practice runs. ; Kessai-hajime (Start of Purification) : On September 13, a ritual is held where the scroll with the image of Konohanasakuya-hime and sacred branches are bestowed. The horse owners and participants then enter a purification period and stay in the shrine's purification hall. Previously, this was done at each horse owner's home, where the family, except for the participants, would leave, and a temporary altar was set up for a period of purification. ; Ato-ma-zoroi (Final Horse Gathering) : On September 15, the horses are adorned with decorations, and the participants draw lots for the actual saddle. The diviners then bestow the necessary horse gear for the festival. ; Sannō-sha Yoimiya-sai (Sannō Shrine festival Eve) : On September 17, the participants visit Sannō Shrine for the bow-taking ceremony, where they receive instructions from the diviners. ; Sannō-sha-sai & Yabusame Matsuri Yoimiya-sai (Sannō Shrine festival & Yabusame festival Eve) : On September 18, the priests, diviners, horse owners, and related participants form a procession to Sannō Shrine, and the Fuji Mountain Mikoshi is carried. : That night, a lottery is held to determine the roles of the horses and the order of their runs for the festival the next day. : The horse gear is managed by the "Ura-bito" (diviners), and the decorative "Otenkō" placed on the horse's forehead is woven from the horse's mane and is believed to be a continuation of the horn-shaped decorations seen on horse-shaped haniwa. [[File:馬蹄占流鏑馬.jpg|thumb|278x278px|Yūma running. The horn-shaped decoration on the horse's forehead is called "Otenkō"]] ; Reitaisai Yabusame Matsuri (festival Yabusame festival) : On September 19, arrows, bows, and targets are given to the horse owners, and the Yabusame is performed in the order of Asauma (morning horse) and Yūma (evening horse), followed by the hoof print divination (batei uranai). The festival concludes with the "San'nō-san's Noppalai" (San'nō's farewell run), where the mountain deity is sent back to the mountain after overseeing the autumn harvest. ; Yabusame Ato-matsuri (Yabusame After festival) : On September 20, the results of the hoof print divination are announced and promptly conveyed to each town. ; Ohimaichi : After the Yabusame festival, the priests visit each town for the "Ohimaichi" ritual based on the divination results. : The ritual is held in various locations, from small gatherings of nearby households to larger events at dining halls or community centers. An altar is set up with the deity's scroll, and participants share food and drink. : In each household, a paper talisman from the priest is received to ensure a year free from fires and disputes. === Tsutsukayū festival === [[File:FujisanSimomiyaOmuroSengenShrine Kayu-ura Ritual.jpg|thumb|Tsutsukayū festival conducted overnight by the hereditary diviner family ({{ill|Yoshi no Ike Onsen|ja|葭之池温泉}})]] In Yamanashi Prefecture, the Tsutsukayū festival is held at various shrines in the Fuji Hokuroku and Yatsugatake regions. At Komuro Sengen Shrine, the Tsutsukayū festival is held overnight from January 14 to early morning January 15. The ritual predicts the year's harvest, weather, sericulture, and the number of Fuji pilgrims, with a notable focus on the latterKatsumata (2007), p.643. The results are published as the Tsutsukayū Divination Mark. After the Tsutsukayū ritual, another divination known as "Terifuri Divination" is performed, where a "Katsunoki" (Nured) piece is placed on the embers and its burning pattern is observed to predict the weather. These results are also published. The Tsutsukayū ritual has been documented in the Sengoku-era diary "Katsuyama-ki" as "Tsutsukai," showing that it has remained largely unchanged since thenKatsumata (2007), p.644. The Tsutsukayū ritual is performed by a hereditary diviner family ({{ill|Yoshi no Ike Onsen|ja|葭之池温泉}}). === Okoe-sai (Changing of the deity's Garments) === Every 60 years, the "Okoe-sai" is held to change the garments of the deity (Konohanasakuya-hime). In the 20th century, this ritual was held in 1950 (Shōwa 25). In the Heisei era, it was held on September 19, 2010 (Heisei 22), and the next ritual is scheduled for 2070. It is believed that seeing the deity outside of this ritual brings misfortune. === Shinmeisai (Sacred Horse festival) === Held annually on Children's Day, May 5, it is known as the "festival of Horses and Children." The festival includes gratitude and memorial services for working horses and past sacred horses, and it features stalls and events from local businesses. == Sacred Horses == [[File:冨士山下宮小室浅間神社 JRA奉納 神馬 瑞桜（ヒカリシャーク）.jpg|thumb|Sacred horse 瑞桜 (Hikari Shark)]] Since 1993, sacred horses have been kept at the shrine to maintain and preserve the Yabusame festival and the hoof print divination ritual. {| class="wikitable" |+History of Sacred Horses ! No. ! Horse name ! Sacred Horse name ! Notes |- | 1 | Hikari Shark | 瑞桜 (Zuio) | |- | 2 | Maxport | | |- | 3 | Towa Takeshiba | | |- | 4 | Daiichi Hijiri | | |- | 5 | Tokin | | |- | 6 | Ichiei Clipper | | |- | 7 | Shiro | | |- | 8 | Kings of the Sun | 旺輝 (Ōki) | |- | 9 | Wise Selection | 賢旺 (Kenō) | Current |} The sacred horses, after their lifetime service, are enshrined in the sacred horse shrine. Every year on May 5, the Shinmeisai is held. In addition to the sacred horses, the shrine also keeps Kiso horses and ponies. == Sessha and Massha == === Daitōmiya Shrine and Hinazuru Shrine === * Deities: {{ill|Prince Moriyoshi|ja|護良親王}} and {{ill|Princess Hinazuru|ja|雛鶴姫}} * festival: May 10 (Katsura festival) [[File:Ootounomiya-katura1.jpg|thumb|216px|Sacred Katsura Tree beside the main shrine, known as the "Daitōmiya Katsura Shrine"]] In the shrine grounds, the sacred Katsura tree, known as "Daitōmiya Katsura Shrine," is revered as a deity. According to ancient documents, in the turmoil of the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, the severed head of {{ill|Prince Moriyoshi|ja|護良親王}} was buried at the root of the sacred Katsura tree by Princess Hinazuru. One such document is a copy of a petition dated September 23, Kenmu 2 (1355), from a descendant of Emperor Seiwa. It describes the burial of Prince Moriyoshi's head at the root of the sacred Katsura tree in the shrine grounds and requests that an image of {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshimitsu|ja|源義光}} be carved and secretly worshipped as Prince Moriyoshi alongside the tree. [[File:Ootounomiya-katura2.jpg|thumb|From right to left: Hinazuru Shrine, Daitōmiya Shrine, Head Mound]] The sacred Katsura tree, estimated to be about 800 years old, is designated a natural monument of Fujiyoshida City. === Shinme Shrine === * deity: White Horse Spirit * festival: May 5 (Shinmeisai) The shrine is dedicated to the sacred horse and the spirits of past horses. The Shinmeisai held on May 5 is known as the "festival of Horses," featuring stalls from local businesses and horse riding experiences for children. === Hie Shrine === * deity: {{ill|Ōyamakui|ja|大山咋神}} * festival: May 5 Locally known as the "Monkey Shrine," the shrine features statues of monkeys, which are believed to be divine messengers. === Gosha Shrine (Daishin Shrine, Yama Shrine, Tennō Shrine, Inari Shrine, Tenjin Shrine) === * Deities: Amaterasu Ōmikami, Ōyamatsumi, Susanoo-no-Mikoto, Ōkuninushi, Sukunabikona, Ukanomitama, Sugawara no Michizane * festival: April 10 The shrine combines five shrines into one. === Ebisu Shrine === * deity: {{ill|Ebisu (mythology)|ja|えびす}} * festival: November 19 (Ebisu-kō) The shrine features an Ebisu statue in the style of Ogata Kōrin. The Ebisu-kō festival is held on November 19. === Benzaiten Shrine === * deity: {{ill|Benzaiten|ja|弁才天}} An ancient shrine utilizing a lava tree mold, preserving an old form of Mount Fuji worship. Surrounded by Maruishi stones. === Arata Hachiman Shrine === * Deities: {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ja|応神天皇}}, {{ill|Tama Yorihime|ja|タマヨリビメ (日向神話)|1=Tamayori-hime (mother of Jimmu)|lt=Tamayori-hime}}, {{ill|Empress Jingū|ja|神功皇后}}, Tanabe Ichike ancestor spirits === Suitengu Shrine === * Deities: Amenominakanushi, Emperor Antoku, Takakura Hirashin no Miya (Kenreimon-in, {{ill|Taira no Tokiko|ja|平徳子}}), Nii no Ama ({{ill|Taira no Tokiko|ja|平時子}}) File:Fuji-omurosengen-horse.jpg|Shinme Shrine, sacred horse statue File:Fuji-omurosengen-monkey.jpg|Hie Shrine "See no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil" statues File:FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengenJinja Benten.jpg|Benzaiten Shrine and Maruishi stones File:FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengenJinja ebisu.jpg|Ebisu Shrine File:FujisanSimomiya OmurosengenJinja Gosya.jpg|Gosha Shrine, five-bay structure, remodeled in the Shōwa era File:FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengenJinja suitengu.jpg|Suitengu Shrine File:FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengenJinja aratahatimangu2.jpg|Arata Hachiman Shrine Haiden File:FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengenJinja aratahatimangu.jpg|Arata Hachiman Shrine Honden File:FujisanSimomiya OmuroSengenjinja Gaku.jpg|Great Torii plaque, calligraphy by {{ill|Tokugawa Munetaka|ja|徳川宗敬}}, 1981 (Shōwa 56) File:FujisanSimomiya OmurosengenJinja torii.jpg|Great Torii, completed in 1981 (Shōwa 56), collapsed in 2004 (Heisei 16) due to a typhoon, rebuilt using original materials in 2010 (Heisei 22), with the pillars replaced with steel in 2020 (Reiwa 2) due to severe damage File:Fujisan Simomiya OmuroSengen Jinja Gaku Sindaisugi.jpg|Shindai-sugi plaque in the Haiden, made from a fragment of a sacred ancient cedar struck by lightning in Tenbun and Kan'ei eras, preserved as recorded in Kai Kokushi File:FujisanSimomiyaOmuroSengenJinja Temizu.jpg|Temizuya, built in 1933 (Shōwa 8) to commemorate the birth of Crown Prince Akihito File:FujisanSimomiyaOmuroSengenJinja KaguraDen.jpg|Kagura-den, built in 1975 (Shōwa 50). A rare stage-style Kagura-den in the area, built to accommodate traditional village Kabuki in place of the district's lack of Kagura File:FujisanSimomiya OmurosengenJinja.jpg|Shrine office, an Edo-period building originally used as a village hall, later moved to the shrine grounds and remodeled into the shrine office. A rotating stage and timber framework remain under the tatami mats in the hall. File:Fuji-omurosengen-pond.jpg|Sacred pond == External Shrines == The Fuji San Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine has two exclave grounds where the Konpira Shrine and Shiroō Shrine are enshrined. === Konpira Shrine === * deity: {{ill|Ōmononushi|ja|大物主}} Located in Shimoyoshida Higashimachi, Fujiyoshida City. This area is known as Furuyoshida Morigumi and is said to be the former site of the Fuji San Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine. During the Sengoku period, there was a purification site for Fuji climbers, where spring water was used for cleansing. A checkpoint was also established here to collect tolls, and it marked the starting point for the Yoshida Route to Mount Fuji, as indicated by the "First Step" stone monument. Gekkōji Temple Aizen and FujisanSimomiya Omurosengen KotohiraShrine.jpg|Konpira Shrine of Fuji San Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine and Aizen Jizō Hall of Gekkō-ji Temple. Their proximity indicates their historical relationship. FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengen KotohiraShrine.jpg|Konpira Shrine Honden Fuji Sekisyo .jpg|Stone monuments, including the "First Step" marker indicating the starting point of the Fuji Yoshida Route, located between Konpira Shrine and Aizen Jizō Hall. === Shiroō Shrine (Shiroō Gongen Shrine) === * Deities: Ōkuninushi, Ōtoshi, Shinatobe Located midway up Otaruyama in Fujiyoshida City. About a 20-minute walk east from {{ill|Arakurayama Sengen Park|ja|新倉山浅間公園}}. The festival is held on August 6, known as the "Bug festival" (虫送り), praying for the expulsion of harmful insects and diseases from the fields and homes of Fujiyoshida. The distributed {{ill|Gohei|ja|御幣}} are placed at the entrances of fields and houses. The name Gongen is a remnant of the syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism. Until the mid-Showa period, many people would climb the mountain holding torches to attend the festival. Hakuou-gongen.jpg|Shiroō Gongen Shrine located in the mountains of Otaruyama == Visitor Information == ; location : Shimoyoshida 3-32-18, Fujiyoshida City, Yamanashi Prefecture : ; Access : Nearest Station: {{ill|Shimoyoshida Station|ja|下吉田駅}}, {{ill|Fujikyu Railway|ja|富士山麓電気鉄道富士急行線}} (5-minute walk) == Notes == {{Reflist}} == References == * {{ill|Katsumata Chikafumi|ja|勝俣鎮夫}}, "The World of the Katsuyama Diary," 'Yamanashi Prefectural History, Volume 2, Medieval,' 2007 == Related Articles == * {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongū Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮冨士浅間神社}} * {{ill|Gekko-ji|ja|月江寺}} * Torii and Haiden |location = {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|ja|山梨県}} {{ill|Fujiyoshida|ja|富士吉田市}} Shimoyoshida 3-32-18 |coordinates = {{coord|35|29|41.36|N|138|48|11.40|E|region:JP-19_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Komuro Sengen Shrine}} |deity = {{ill|Konohanasakuya-hime|ja|コノハナノサクヤビメ}} |神体 = Mount Fuji |Rank = Former {{ill|Gōsha|ja|近代Rank制度#諸社}}
{{ill|Beppyo Shrine|ja|別表神社}} |established = (伝) {{ill|Daidō|ja|大同 (日本)}} 2 (807) |main hall = |alternative name = Shimomiya-san |札所等 = |festival= Yabusame festival (Horse Hoof Divination Ritual) {{ill|September 19|ja|9月19日}} |festival = Tsutsukayū festival January 14
Shinmeisai May 5 |map = {{location map|Japan Yamanashi|lat_deg=35|lat_min=29|lat_sec=41.3|lon_deg=138|lon_min=48|lon_sec=11.4|label=冨士山下宮小室浅間神社|position=bottom|width=200|float=center|caption=|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=20}} {{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=11|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|coord={{coord|35|29|41.36|N|138|48|11.40|E}}}} }} '''{{ill|Omuro Sengen Shrine (Yamanashi)|lt=Omuro Sengen Shrine|ja|冨士山下宮小室浅間神社}}''' (冨士山下宮小室浅間神社) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Fujiyoshida|ja|富士吉田市}}, {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|ja|山梨県}}. The former Rank under the {{ill|Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|ja|近代Rank制度}} was that of a Gōsha, and it is now designated as a Beppyo Shrine under the jurisdiction of the {{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|ja|神社本庁}}. It is one of the many {{ill|Sengen shrines|ja|浅間神社}} across Japan. The former name was '''Fuji San Shimomiya Sengen Shrine'''慶応四年辰年八月の「富士山下宮社地取調書上帳」. The shrine is dedicated to the {{ill|Ubusunagami|ja|産土神|1=Ubusunagami}} of the Fuji Hokuroku region and the entire {{ill|Fujiyoshida|ja|富士吉田市}}, serving as the {{ill|Chinjugami|ja|総鎮守}} of the three villages of Kamiyoshida, Shimoyoshida, and Matsuyama. {{ill|Shinme|ja|神馬}} are kept at the shrine. Locally, it is also referred to as "Shimomiya-san" or "Shimosengen." == Overview == Throughout the year, divination ('''占い''') and oracles ('''神籤(おみくじ）''') play a significant role in the festivals held at the shrine. This includes the "Horse Hoof Divination Yabusame festival" and the "Tsutsukayū festival," which reflect the ancient Fuji worship deeply rooted in the lives of local residents. According to the {{ill|Kai Kokushi|ja|甲斐国志}}, the shrine is the birthplace deity of Kamiyoshida, Shimoyoshida, and Matsuyama villages. Even as other shrines have increased in the surrounding area, the practice of {{ill|Hatsumiya Mairi|ja|初宮参り}} for newborns remains strong, indicating the deep faith of local residents. == Deities == * {{ill|Konohanasakuya-hime|ja|コノハナノサクヤビメ}} == History == According to the shrine legend, in Enryaku 12 (793), {{ill|Sakanoue no Tamuramaro|ja|坂上田村麻呂}}, during his eastern expedition, prayed for victory while worshipping Mount Fuji from Yoshida. After his victory, in gratitude for the divine favor, he built the shrine in Daidō 2 (807). Early records mention the shrine as "Miya" (宮). Until the detailed village survey book of Hōei 3 (1708), it was recorded as "Sengen Miya." Originally, the settlement of Shimoyoshida was located in present-day Shimoyoshida Higashimachi, where it was enshrined at the current location of the {{ill|Higashimachi Kotohira Shrine|ja|東町金毘羅神社}}. Due to frequent snowmelt damage, the settlement and shrine were relocated to their current location, backed by the Kenmaruo Lava Flow{{Cite book|title=下吉田の民俗|date=1990.3.25|year=1990|publisher=富士吉田市教育委員会}}. In Kenmu 2 (1355) on September 23, the head of {{ill|Prince Moriyoshi|ja|護良親王}}, a descendant of Emperor Seiwa, was buried at the root of a sacred katsura tree, and a petition was left behind. In Tenshō 4 (1576), the towns of both Kamiyoshida and Shimoyoshida were completely burned down during the battle between the {{ill|Hōjō clan|ja|北条氏}} and {{ill|Oyamada clan|ja|小山田氏}} ({{ill|Katsuyama-ki|ja|勝山記}}). During the Edo period, the shrine was also the guardian of the largest temple in the Fuji Hokuroku area, {{ill|Gekko-ji|ja|月江寺}}, and until the Meiji era, recitations by Gekko-ji monks were part of the shrine festivals. In Kan'ei 3 (1626) on April 6, a sacred ancient cedar tree in the shrine grounds was struck by lightning and burned ({{ill|Kai Kokushi|ja|甲斐国志}}). A fragment of this tree is displayed as a plaque in the current haiden. The haiden dates back to the Tenshō era (1573-1593). The honden, built by {{ill|Gunai Daiku Nakama|ja|郡内大工仲間}} master carpenter Kayanuma Yasaburō in Meiwa 4 (1767), is the largest single-bay shrine building in Yamanashi Prefecture. This honden served as a model for subsequent shrine buildings in the area. Although it is not registered as a cultural property, it is significant in its architecture. [[File:Fujisan Simomiya Omurosengen Jinjya 冨士山下宮小室浅間神社 本殿.jpg|thumb|250x250px|Honden. Single-bay Irimoya-zukuri style with Karahafu at the front. It is the largest single-bay honden in Yamanashi Prefecture. The eaves are enclosed with covering walls.]] During the Meiji period, the shrine transferred its parishioner area of Kamiyoshida to the {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongū Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮冨士浅間神社}} and changed its name from "Fuji San Shimomiya Sengen Shrine" to the current "Komuro Sengen Shrine." In line with this change, the enshrined deities were unified from "Sengen Daimyōjin, Amaterasu Ōmikami, Inukai Daimyōjin, Aitaka Daigongen, Shinra Saburō Yoshimitsu (Prince Moriyoshi)" to "Konohanasakuya-hime (Sengen Ōkami)." The shrine crest was also changed from "Shuro no Ha" to "Yamato Yaezakura." Amaterasu Ōmikami was moved to the Gosha Shrine, and Prince Moriyoshi was enshrined separately in the Daitōmiya Shrine. In 1957, the shrine exchanged its grounds and municipal land on Otaruyama with the neighboring Shimoyoshida First Elementary School for playground expansion. In the same year, it was designated a Beppyo Shrine. === Origin of the name "Shimomiya" === The term "Shimomiya" refers to the lower shrine in relation to Mount Fuji, with no specific upper shrine. There are several theories as to why it is called "Shimomiya." # Originally referred to simply as "Miya," it was called "Shimomiya" to distinguish it from other Sengen shrines that began to enshrine Sengen Ōkami in the villages, referring to the shrine lower in relation to Mount Fuji{{Cite web|和書|title=富士山下宮小室浅間神社　由諸|url=http://www.fgo.jp/~yabusame/rekisi.htm|website=www.fgo.jp|accessdate=2019-09-09}}. # The term "Shimomiya" was used by people around Lake Kawaguchi to refer to the Fuji Yoshida area, distinguishing it from {{ill|Kawaguchi Sengen Shrine|ja|河口浅間神社}}. # The term "Shimomiya" referred to the lower shrine in relation to the Komuro Sengen Shrine at the second station of Mount Fuji (now the former main shrine of the {{ill|Fuji Omuro Sengen Shrine|ja|冨士御室浅間神社}}). This theory, however, has been widely spread but is now considered a folk belief, as shown by the following points: #* Both shrines have different origins and histories. #* The {{ill|Kai Kokushi|ja|甲斐国志}} mentions the Komuro Sengen Shrine's satomiya in Katsuyama, but there is no mention of the relationship with Shimomiya Sengen. #* The Komuro Sengen Shrine at the second station was easily acquired by Katsuyama in Fujikawaguchiko as an exclave. #* The shrine building from the second station was moved to the satomiya grounds in Katsuyama. #* The relationship with the Komuro Sengen Shrine at the second station was not proven, so it was excluded from the list of components for the Mount Fuji World Cultural Heritage designation (it was seen more as a birthplace, tutelary, or guardian deity, deeply rooted in local life rather than Fuji worship). #* During the Meiji period, another shrine in the same city, Ōasumi's {{ill|Komuro Sengen Shrine (Fujiyoshida Ōasumi)|ja|小室浅間神社 (富士吉田市大明見)}}, was renamed to "Komuro Sengen Shrine." #* The Yabusame festival was traditionally held together, but the records and descriptions, such as the {{ill|Katsuyama-ki|ja|勝山記}} and {{ill|Myōhō-ji-ki|ja|妙法寺記}}, do not mention horse hoof divination or divination rituals in Katsuyama. #* The place where the Yabusame was held is described as "Rokubanba near Nakano Chaya" in theory 3, but it is actually "Nakano Chaya near the second station," which is far apart, showing no connection between Rokubanba and the Komuro Sengen Shrine at the second station. #* The Yabusame was performed by various shrines and villages in the Fuji Hokuroku area. Over time, the Rokubanba became the Nagabanba, and the ceremonies became more localized. #* As mentioned below, there is confusion between "Shimomiya" and "Shimoyashima." === Confusion between "Shimoyashima" and "Shimomiya" === In {{ill|Fujiyoshida|ja|富士吉田市}}, the {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongū Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮冨士浅間神社}} is located in Kamiyoshida, while the Komuro Sengen Shrine is in Shimoyoshida. Therefore, it is easy to mistake the Komuro Sengen Shrine as the "Shimomiya" in contrast to the "Hongū" of Kitaguchi. In modern times, the Kitaguchi Hongū is referred to as "Kami Sengen" or "Kami Sen," and the Komuro Sengen Shrine as "Shimoyashima" or "Shimo Sen," which further perpetuates the confusion. However, '''"Shimoyashima" originally referred to the {{ill|Kitaguchi Hongū Fuji Sengen Shrine|ja|北口本宮冨士浅間神社}} rather than the Fuji San Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine'''{{Cite web|和書|url=https://www.pref.yamanashi.jp/fujisan/rebirth/documents/fujisanmichi-omote.pdf|title=富士参詣富士山道表|accessdate=2019.02|publisher=山梨県富士山世界文化遺産保存活用推進協議会}}. For example, the 'Hachiyō Kunsun-zu' from Enpō 8 (1680), which depicts the Yoshida Route to Mount Fuji, refers to the current Kitaguchi Hongū grounds as "Shimoyashima"{{Cite journal|author=串田優子 伊藤裕久|year=2006|title=北口本宮冨士浅間神社境内空間の変遷過程|journal=日本建築学会計画系論文集|volume=第604号|page=159−16S}}. Additionally, the 'Kai Kokushi' from Bunka 11 (1814) describes the Komuro Sengen Shrine at the second station (now Fuji Omuro Sengen Shrine) as "Kami Sengen," and the shrine at Kitaguchi as "Shimoyashima," with the shrine at Shimoyoshida referred to as "Shimomiya Sengen." From the above, it is clear that "Shimoyashima" and "Shimomiya Sengen" were separate entities. However, after the transfer of the parishioner area of Kamiyoshida to Kitaguchi Hongū, the relationship with the Komuro Sengen Shrine at the second station in Katsuyama of Fujikawaguchiko weakened. Thus, the term "Kami Sengen" ceased to be used for the second station shrine, leading to the Kitaguchi Hongū being referred to as "Kami Sengen" and the Komuro Sengen Shrine as "Shimoyashima," with the latter being renamed to "Komuro Sengen Shrine" during the Meiji period, further perpetuating the confusion between "Shimoyashima" and "Shimomiya." == festivals == === Yabusame festival === [[File:小室浅間神社（下宮）神馬舎.jpg|thumb|200px|Shinmesha and the Shinme kept in it]] [[File:Fujiyosida-Yabusame-FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengen.webm|thumb|Yabusame at Fuji San Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine, taken on September 19, 2020]] The Yabusame festival, designated as an Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Yamanashi Prefecture, is held on September 19, the day of the {{ill|Reisai|ja|festival}}, and is famous for the "Horse Hoof Divination" (''batei uranai''). Locally known as "Umatobakashi" (甲州弁: to run the horse), the Yabusame festival is said to have started with a mid-period horseback riding in Chōkan 2 (1164), with the formal Yabusame festival beginning in Angen 2 (1176). The formal practices of the festival, including Asauma (morning horse) and Yuuma (evening horse), were established in Kenkyū 3 (1192), and the festival date was set to September 19 in Eikyō 12 (1440). In the shrine grounds, the sacred horses used for Yabusame are kept. These horses are donated by the Japan Racing Association. This festival is unique from the generally known Yabusame, being closely tied to agricultural faith and the lives of local residents. It features divination by "Ura-bito" (diviners) who interpret the horse hoof prints (batei uranai), oracles (mikuji) to seek divine will, and a week-long purification ritual called "kiribi." The horses for Yabusame are donated by parishioners, and the festival begins with the application and selection of the horses, known as "Uma-dashi no Kushi-uranai," held on January 15, the day after the Tsutsukayū festival. The festival includes the "Hatsu-ma-zoroi" on September 1, "Naka-ma-zoroi" on September 9, "Kessai-hajime" on September 13, "Ato-ma-zoroi" on September 15, "Tenjinsha-sankō and Tenjinsha Sannō-sai" on September 18, the "Reitaisai Yabusame Matsuri" on September 19, and the "Ato-matsuri" on September 20. In the past, families without horses would borrow them from local or neighboring farmers. However, with the decline in horse ownership, the shrine now keeps horses for the festival. Originally held at the "Rokubanba near Nakano Chaya," halfway between the Mount Fuji climbing gate and Umagaeshi, the festival has been performed at the "Honmachi Nakamu Ra Horse Grounds" since the late Edo period. The current horse grounds were used by 1848, as shown in the "festival map of September 19" from that year. [[File:富士山神輿.JPG|200px|thumb|right|Fuji Mountain Mikoshi]] In 2007, after a hiatus, the Fuji Mountain Mikoshi was revived, and its procession takes place on the eve of the festival, September 18. ; Uma-dashi no Kushi-uranai (Horse Selection Divination) : Early morning on January 15, after the results of the Tsutsukayū festival divination are announced, the application for Yabusame horses begins. The horse owners and horses are selected through a divination ritual held at noon. Traditionally, 30 to 60 applications were made for the six horses, and being selected as a horse owner was a great honor. Recently, the number of applications has been lower than the required number. ; Hatsu-ma-zoroi (First Horse Gathering) : On September 1, all horses for the festival gather at the shrine, where a ritual is performed. Each horse owner draws a lot for the practice saddle and receives a set of practice horse gear from the diviners. The horses are then shown to the public and trained (currently, the sacred horses kept at the shrine practice in the shrine grounds). ; Naka-ma-zoroi (Middle Horse Gathering) : On September 9, the horses gather again for a ritual and practice runs. ; Kessai-hajime (Start of Purification) : On September 13, a ritual is held where the scroll with the image of Konohanasakuya-hime and sacred branches are bestowed. The horse owners and participants then enter a purification period and stay in the shrine's purification hall. Previously, this was done at each horse owner's home, where the family, except for the participants, would leave, and a temporary altar was set up for a period of purification. ; Ato-ma-zoroi (Final Horse Gathering) : On September 15, the horses are adorned with decorations, and the participants draw lots for the actual saddle. The diviners then bestow the necessary horse gear for the festival. ; Sannō-sha Yoimiya-sai (Sannō Shrine festival Eve) : On September 17, the participants visit Sannō Shrine for the bow-taking ceremony, where they receive instructions from the diviners. ; Sannō-sha-sai & Yabusame Matsuri Yoimiya-sai (Sannō Shrine festival & Yabusame festival Eve) : On September 18, the priests, diviners, horse owners, and related participants form a procession to Sannō Shrine, and the Fuji Mountain Mikoshi is carried. : That night, a lottery is held to determine the roles of the horses and the order of their runs for the festival the next day. : The horse gear is managed by the "Ura-bito" (diviners), and the decorative "Otenkō" placed on the horse's forehead is woven from the horse's mane and is believed to be a continuation of the horn-shaped decorations seen on horse-shaped haniwa. [[File:馬蹄占流鏑馬.jpg|thumb|278x278px|Yūma running. The horn-shaped decoration on the horse's forehead is called "Otenkō"]] ; Reitaisai Yabusame Matsuri (festival Yabusame festival) : On September 19, arrows, bows, and targets are given to the horse owners, and the Yabusame is performed in the order of Asauma (morning horse) and Yūma (evening horse), followed by the hoof print divination (batei uranai). The festival concludes with the "San'nō-san's Noppalai" (San'nō's farewell run), where the mountain deity is sent back to the mountain after overseeing the autumn harvest. ; Yabusame Ato-matsuri (Yabusame After festival) : On September 20, the results of the hoof print divination are announced and promptly conveyed to each town. ; Ohimaichi : After the Yabusame festival, the priests visit each town for the "Ohimaichi" ritual based on the divination results. : The ritual is held in various locations, from small gatherings of nearby households to larger events at dining halls or community centers. An altar is set up with the deity's scroll, and participants share food and drink. : In each household, a paper talisman from the priest is received to ensure a year free from fires and disputes. === Tsutsukayū festival === [[File:FujisanSimomiyaOmuroSengenShrine Kayu-ura Ritual.jpg|thumb|Tsutsukayū festival conducted overnight by the hereditary diviner family ({{ill|Yoshi no Ike Onsen|ja|葭之池温泉}})]] In Yamanashi Prefecture, the Tsutsukayū festival is held at various shrines in the Fuji Hokuroku and Yatsugatake regions. At Komuro Sengen Shrine, the Tsutsukayū festival is held overnight from January 14 to early morning January 15. The ritual predicts the year's harvest, weather, sericulture, and the number of Fuji pilgrims, with a notable focus on the latterKatsumata (2007), p.643. The results are published as the Tsutsukayū Divination Mark. After the Tsutsukayū ritual, another divination known as "Terifuri Divination" is performed, where a "Katsunoki" (Nured) piece is placed on the embers and its burning pattern is observed to predict the weather. These results are also published. The Tsutsukayū ritual has been documented in the Sengoku-era diary "Katsuyama-ki" as "Tsutsukai," showing that it has remained largely unchanged since thenKatsumata (2007), p.644. The Tsutsukayū ritual is performed by a hereditary diviner family ({{ill|Yoshi no Ike Onsen|ja|葭之池温泉}}). === Okoe-sai (Changing of the deity's Garments) === Every 60 years, the "Okoe-sai" is held to change the garments of the deity (Konohanasakuya-hime). In the 20th century, this ritual was held in 1950 (Shōwa 25). In the Heisei era, it was held on September 19, 2010 (Heisei 22), and the next ritual is scheduled for 2070. It is believed that seeing the deity outside of this ritual brings misfortune. === Shinmeisai (Sacred Horse festival) === Held annually on Children's Day, May 5, it is known as the "festival of Horses and Children." The festival includes gratitude and memorial services for working horses and past sacred horses, and it features stalls and events from local businesses. == Sacred Horses == [[File:冨士山下宮小室浅間神社 JRA奉納 神馬 瑞桜（ヒカリシャーク）.jpg|thumb|Sacred horse 瑞桜 (Hikari Shark)]] Since 1993, sacred horses have been kept at the shrine to maintain and preserve the Yabusame festival and the hoof print divination ritual. {| class="wikitable" |+History of Sacred Horses ! No. ! Horse name ! Sacred Horse name ! Notes |- | 1 | Hikari Shark | 瑞桜 (Zuio) | |- | 2 | Maxport | | |- | 3 | Towa Takeshiba | | |- | 4 | Daiichi Hijiri | | |- | 5 | Tokin | | |- | 6 | Ichiei Clipper | | |- | 7 | Shiro | | |- | 8 | Kings of the Sun | 旺輝 (Ōki) | |- | 9 | Wise Selection | 賢旺 (Kenō) | Current |} The sacred horses, after their lifetime service, are enshrined in the sacred horse shrine. Every year on May 5, the Shinmeisai is held. In addition to the sacred horses, the shrine also keeps Kiso horses and ponies. == Sessha and Massha == === Daitōmiya Shrine and Hinazuru Shrine === * Deities: {{ill|Prince Moriyoshi|ja|護良親王}} and {{ill|Princess Hinazuru|ja|雛鶴姫}} * festival: May 10 (Katsura festival) [[File:Ootounomiya-katura1.jpg|thumb|216px|Sacred Katsura Tree beside the main shrine, known as the "Daitōmiya Katsura Shrine"]] In the shrine grounds, the sacred Katsura tree, known as "Daitōmiya Katsura Shrine," is revered as a deity. According to ancient documents, in the turmoil of the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}}, the severed head of {{ill|Prince Moriyoshi|ja|護良親王}} was buried at the root of the sacred Katsura tree by Princess Hinazuru. One such document is a copy of a petition dated September 23, Kenmu 2 (1355), from a descendant of Emperor Seiwa. It describes the burial of Prince Moriyoshi's head at the root of the sacred Katsura tree in the shrine grounds and requests that an image of {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshimitsu|ja|源義光}} be carved and secretly worshipped as Prince Moriyoshi alongside the tree. [[File:Ootounomiya-katura2.jpg|thumb|From right to left: Hinazuru Shrine, Daitōmiya Shrine, Head Mound]] The sacred Katsura tree, estimated to be about 800 years old, is designated a natural monument of Fujiyoshida City. === Shinme Shrine === * deity: White Horse Spirit * festival: May 5 (Shinmeisai) The shrine is dedicated to the sacred horse and the spirits of past horses. The Shinmeisai held on May 5 is known as the "festival of Horses," featuring stalls from local businesses and horse riding experiences for children. === Hie Shrine === * deity: {{ill|Ōyamakui|ja|大山咋神}} * festival: May 5 Locally known as the "Monkey Shrine," the shrine features statues of monkeys, which are believed to be divine messengers. === Gosha Shrine (Daishin Shrine, Yama Shrine, Tennō Shrine, Inari Shrine, Tenjin Shrine) === * Deities: Amaterasu Ōmikami, Ōyamatsumi, Susanoo-no-Mikoto, Ōkuninushi, Sukunabikona, Ukanomitama, Sugawara no Michizane * festival: April 10 The shrine combines five shrines into one. === Ebisu Shrine === * deity: {{ill|Ebisu (mythology)|ja|えびす}} * festival: November 19 (Ebisu-kō) The shrine features an Ebisu statue in the style of Ogata Kōrin. The Ebisu-kō festival is held on November 19. === Benzaiten Shrine === * deity: {{ill|Benzaiten|ja|弁才天}} An ancient shrine utilizing a lava tree mold, preserving an old form of Mount Fuji worship. Surrounded by Maruishi stones. === Arata Hachiman Shrine === * Deities: {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ja|応神天皇}}, {{ill|Tama Yorihime|ja|タマヨリビメ (日向神話)|1=Tamayori-hime (mother of Jimmu)|lt=Tamayori-hime}}, {{ill|Empress Jingū|ja|神功皇后}}, Tanabe Ichike ancestor spirits === Suitengu Shrine === * Deities: Amenominakanushi, Emperor Antoku, Takakura Hirashin no Miya (Kenreimon-in, {{ill|Taira no Tokiko|ja|平徳子}}), Nii no Ama ({{ill|Taira no Tokiko|ja|平時子}}) File:Fuji-omurosengen-horse.jpg|Shinme Shrine, sacred horse statue File:Fuji-omurosengen-monkey.jpg|Hie Shrine "See no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil" statues File:FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengenJinja Benten.jpg|Benzaiten Shrine and Maruishi stones File:FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengenJinja ebisu.jpg|Ebisu Shrine File:FujisanSimomiya OmurosengenJinja Gosya.jpg|Gosha Shrine, five-bay structure, remodeled in the Shōwa era File:FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengenJinja suitengu.jpg|Suitengu Shrine File:FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengenJinja aratahatimangu2.jpg|Arata Hachiman Shrine Haiden File:FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengenJinja aratahatimangu.jpg|Arata Hachiman Shrine Honden File:FujisanSimomiya OmuroSengenjinja Gaku.jpg|Great Torii plaque, calligraphy by {{ill|Tokugawa Munetaka|ja|徳川宗敬}}, 1981 (Shōwa 56) File:FujisanSimomiya OmurosengenJinja torii.jpg|Great Torii, completed in 1981 (Shōwa 56), collapsed in 2004 (Heisei 16) due to a typhoon, rebuilt using original materials in 2010 (Heisei 22), with the pillars replaced with steel in 2020 (Reiwa 2) due to severe damage File:Fujisan Simomiya OmuroSengen Jinja Gaku Sindaisugi.jpg|Shindai-sugi plaque in the Haiden, made from a fragment of a sacred ancient cedar struck by lightning in Tenbun and Kan'ei eras, preserved as recorded in Kai Kokushi File:FujisanSimomiyaOmuroSengenJinja Temizu.jpg|Temizuya, built in 1933 (Shōwa 8) to commemorate the birth of Crown Prince Akihito File:FujisanSimomiyaOmuroSengenJinja KaguraDen.jpg|Kagura-den, built in 1975 (Shōwa 50). A rare stage-style Kagura-den in the area, built to accommodate traditional village Kabuki in place of the district's lack of Kagura File:FujisanSimomiya OmurosengenJinja.jpg|Shrine office, an Edo-period building originally used as a village hall, later moved to the shrine grounds and remodeled into the shrine office. A rotating stage and timber framework remain under the tatami mats in the hall. File:Fuji-omurosengen-pond.jpg|Sacred pond == External Shrines == The Fuji San Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine has two exclave grounds where the Konpira Shrine and Shiroō Shrine are enshrined. === Konpira Shrine === * deity: {{ill|Ōmononushi|ja|大物主}} Located in Shimoyoshida Higashimachi, Fujiyoshida City. This area is known as Furuyoshida Morigumi and is said to be the former site of the Fuji San Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine. During the Sengoku period, there was a purification site for Fuji climbers, where spring water was used for cleansing. A checkpoint was also established here to collect tolls, and it marked the starting point for the Yoshida Route to Mount Fuji, as indicated by the "First Step" stone monument. Gekkōji Temple Aizen and FujisanSimomiya Omurosengen KotohiraShrine.jpg|Konpira Shrine of Fuji San Shimomiya Komuro Sengen Shrine and Aizen Jizō Hall of Gekkō-ji Temple. Their proximity indicates their historical relationship. FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengen KotohiraShrine.jpg|Konpira Shrine Honden Fuji Sekisyo .jpg|Stone monuments, including the "First Step" marker indicating the starting point of the Fuji Yoshida Route, located between Konpira Shrine and Aizen Jizō Hall. === Shiroō Shrine (Shiroō Gongen Shrine) === * Deities: Ōkuninushi, Ōtoshi, Shinatobe Located midway up Otaruyama in Fujiyoshida City. About a 20-minute walk east from {{ill|Arakurayama Sengen Park|ja|新倉山浅間公園}}. The festival is held on August 6, known as the "Bug festival" (虫送り), praying for the expulsion of harmful insects and diseases from the fields and homes of Fujiyoshida. The distributed {{ill|Gohei|ja|御幣}} are placed at the entrances of fields and houses. The name Gongen is a remnant of the syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism. Until the mid-Showa period, many people would climb the mountain holding torches to attend the festival. Hakuou-gongen.jpg|Shiroō Gongen Shrine located in the mountains of Otaruyama == Visitor Information == ; location : Shimoyoshida 3-32-18, Fujiyoshida City, Yamanashi Prefecture : ; Access : Nearest Station: {{ill|Shimoyoshida Station|ja|下吉田駅}}, {{ill|Fujikyu Railway|ja|富士山麓電気鉄道富士急行線}} (5-minute walk) == Notes == {{Reflist}} == References == * {{ill|Katsumata Chikafumi|ja|勝俣鎮夫}}, "The World of {{神社 |名称 = 冨士山下宮小室浅間神社 |画像 = [[ファイル:Fujisan Shimomiya Omuro Sengen jinja torii — 2021.jpg|250px|]]
鳥居と拝殿 |所在地 = [[山梨県]][[富士吉田市]]下吉田3丁目32番18号 |位置 = {{ウィキ座標2段度分秒|35|29|41.36|N|138|48|11.40|E|region:JP-19_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=小室浅間神社}} |祭神 = [[コノハナノサクヤビメ|木花咲耶姫命]] |神体 = 富士山 |社格 = 旧[[近代社格制度#諸社|郷社]]
[[別表神社]] |創建 = （伝）[[大同 (日本)|大同]]2年（[[807年]]） |本殿 = |別名 = 下宮さん |札所等 = |例祭 = 流鏑馬祭（馬蹄占い神事）[[9月19日]] |神事 = 筒粥祭１月１４日
神馬祭５月　５日 |地図 = {{Location map|Japan Yamanashi|lat_deg=35|lat_min=29|lat_sec=41.3|lon_deg=138|lon_min=48|lon_sec=11.4|label=冨士山下宮小室浅間神社|position=bottom|width=200|float=center|caption=|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=20}} {{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=11|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|coord={{coord|35|29|41.36|N|138|48|11.40|E}}}} }} '''冨士山下宮小室浅間神社'''（ふじさんしもみやおむろせんげんじんじゃ）は、[[山梨県]][[富士吉田市]]にある[[神社]]。[[近代社格制度|旧社格]]は[[近代社格制度#諸社|郷社]]で、現在は[[神社本庁]]の[[別表神社]]。全国にある[[浅間神社]]の一社。旧称'''冨士山下宮浅間神社'''慶応四年辰年八月の「富士山下宮社地取調書上帳」。[[法人登記|登記]]上の[[宗教法人]]名称は'''小室浅間神社'''（おむろせんげんじんじゃ)。 富士北麓地域・富士吉田一円の[[産土神|'''産土大神''']]で、上吉田・下吉田・松山の三郷の'''[[総鎮守]]。''' [[神馬]]の飼育をしている。地元では「下宮（しもみや）さん」「下浅間（しもせんげん）」とも呼ばれる。 == 概要 == 年間を通じて、祭事に「'''[[占い]]'''」「'''[[おみくじ|神籤(おみくじ）]]'''」が重要な位置をしめており、後述する祭礼である「'''馬蹄占（ばていうらない）をする流鏑馬祭'''」と「'''筒粥祭'''」の占いから地域住民の生活に密着した古い富士山信仰が窺える。 『[[甲斐国志]]』に「此ノ社、古ヘ上下吉田及ビ松山三村ノ産子ナリ。後、各村一祠ヲ立テ祭ル今モ猶上吉田ニハ、子生マレテ百日ノ後、社参スルニ先ズ下宮ニ参詣ス。」とあり、周辺に他の神社が増えても赤子の無事の成長を祈る[[初宮参り]]が盛んで、地域住人の信仰を受けていることが伝わる。 == 祭神 == * [[コノハナノサクヤビメ|木花咲耶姫命]] == 歴史 == 社伝によれば、[[延暦]]12年（[[793年]]）、征夷大将軍[[坂上田村麻呂]]が東征の際、吉田の地より[[富士山]]を遙拝して戦勝を祈願し、戦勝後の[[大同 (日本)|大同]]2年（[[807年]]）、神恩に感謝して社殿を造営したのに始まるという。 古い記録では「宮」と記されており、[[宝永]]3年（1708年）の村差出明細帳までは「浅間宮」と記載されていた。 かつて下吉田の集落は現在の下吉田東町にあり、現在境外末社である東町金毘羅神社のある地に祀られていたが、雪代被害が多く現在の地に集落と共に移転し、剣丸尾溶岩を背負う形で移された{{Cite book|title=下吉田の民俗|date=1990.3.25|year=1990|publisher=富士吉田市教育委員会}} と伝わる。 [[建武 (日本)|建武]]2年（1355年）9月23日[[清和天皇]]遠孫を称する家臣、[[護良親王|大塔宮護良親王]]の首を桂の神木の根元に葬り、祈請書を残す。 [[天正]]4年（1576年）北条氏と小山田氏の戦いで上下両吉田の町と全焼する（[[勝山記|勝山記・妙法寺記]]）。 江戸時代、富士北麓最大規模の寺院、[[月江寺]]の鎮守でもあり、明治までは祭礼で月江寺僧の諷経が行われていた。 [[寛永]]3年（1626年）4月6日、社中の杉の古木が雷火で燃える（[[甲斐国志]]）現在の拝殿にその一辺が[[扁額]]となって飾られている。 拝殿は[[天正]]年間（[[ユリウス暦]][[1573年]]から[[グレゴリオ暦]][[1593年]]）の造り。 本殿は[[明和]]4年（1767年）'''[[郡内大工仲間]]'''は御役大工棟梁萱沼弥左衛門による建築で、山梨県最大の一間社本殿となる。この本殿は以降の郡内大工仲間の本殿建築に図面が参考・下地にされ、郡内域に中小同様の社殿が建設された。文化財の登録はしていない。 [[ファイル:Fujisan Simomiya Omurosengen Jinjya 冨士山下宮小室浅間神社 本殿.jpg|thumb|250px|本殿。一間社入母屋造り向拝唐破風付き。山梨県最大の一間社本殿である。軒下が覆壁に囲われている。]] 明治に入り氏子地域であった上吉田を[[北口本宮冨士浅間神社]]に割譲し、それまでの「冨士山下宮浅間神社」から現在の「小室浅間神社」に改称した。 それに合わせて、祭神も江戸末期まで記名されていた本殿の「浅間大明神、天照大神、犬飼大明神、愛鷹大権現、新羅三郎義光（仮借、[[護良親王]]）」を「[[コノハナノサクヤビメ|木花咲耶姫命]]（浅間大神）」一柱に統一し、表の神紋を「棕櫚の葉」から「大和八重桜」に変更した。 天照大神は末社の五社神社に、護良親王は大塔宮社に分社された。 1957年（[[昭和]]32年）、隣接する下吉田第一小学校の校庭拡張の為、境内地と尾垂山の市有地を交換した。また同年、別表神社に列格。 === 下宮の由来 === 富士山に対する「'''下宮'''」であり、具体的な上宮は存在しない。 なぜ下宮と呼ばれるのかについては諸説ある。 # 元々単に「宮」と呼称されていたが、上吉田の諏訪ノ森にある諏訪神社境内に新たに祀られた[[北口本宮冨士浅間神社]]等、各村々で浅間大神を祀り始めたため区別する必要から、富士の北麓では古くから富士山の方角を上と呼ぶ為、他の浅間神社より富士山の下手に在る宮として「下宮」と呼称されるようになった{{Cite web|和書|title=富士山下宮小室浅間神社　由諸|url=http://www.fgo.jp/~yabusame/rekisi.htm|website=www.fgo.jp|accessdate=2019-09-09}}。 # 元々単に「宮」と呼称されていたが、昔から河口湖の人々が富士吉田方面を下（しも）と呼んでいる為、[[河口浅間神社]]と比較して「下宮」と呼ばれるようになった。 # 富士山二合目にある小室浅間神社（現・[[冨士御室浅間神社]]旧本宮）を「上宮」とし、それに対する呼称「里宮」ともいわれた『日本の神々』一宮浅間神社項。。ただこの説は広く流布しているが'''[[俗説]]'''で、以下の点から現在否定されている。 #* 両社は流鏑馬を含め由緒由来が異なる。 #* 「甲斐国志」に富士河口湖町勝山には小室浅間神社里宮の記述があるのに対し、下宮浅間には小室浅間神社との関連つける記述が一切ない。 #* 二合目の小室浅間神社社地を富士河口湖町勝山が飛び地として問題なく得た。 #* 二合目の社殿を富士河口湖勝山の里宮境内に移築した。 #* 二合目小室浅間神社との関連が立証されず富士山世界文化遺産の構成候補から外れた。（[[富士講]]による富士山信仰というよりも、[[産土神|産土]]・[[氏神]]・[[鎮守神|鎮守]]的な要素、生活に根差した富士山信仰が強く登録にあたり吉田・船津口登山道の一環として採用できなかった） #* 同富士吉田市内大明見の[[小室浅間神社 (富士吉田市大明見)|阿曽谷宮守神社]]が同時期に同じ社名「小室浅間神社」に改称した。 #* 流鏑馬祭を共同で執り行っていたと伝わるが、「勝山記・妙法寺記」などから途絶える明治までにも富士河口湖勝山の流鏑馬に「馬蹄占」「占い」をしていた記録・記述がない。 #*流鏑馬祭を行っていた場所が「二合目小室浅間神社近くの騮ヶ馬場」と３の説にあるが、実際は「中の茶屋の近くにあった騮ヶ馬場」であり場所が大きく違い、騮ヶ馬場の場所は二合目小室浅間神社と関係がない事。 #*流鏑馬は富士北麓全域の各神社・村々合同で行われており、騮ヶ馬場以降、長馬場と時代が下るにつれ、それぞれの地域に分散化していることが分かってきている。 #* 下述にあるが近代「下浅間」と「下宮浅間」が混同されている。 === 下浅間と下宮浅間の混同 === 富士吉田市内には北口本宮冨士浅間神社が上吉田に、この小室浅間神社が下吉田にあるため、北口本宮の呼称「本宮」に対して当神社を「下宮」と呼称しているとの誤解を招きやすい。現代では北口本宮を「上浅間（かみせんげん）」や「上浅（かみせん）」、小室浅間神社を「下浅間（しもせんげん）」や「下浅（しもせん）」と呼ぶことが定着してしまっていることもそれに拍車をかけている。 しかし、'''本来「下浅間」とは冨士山下宮小室浅間神社ではなく北口本宮冨士浅間神社を指している'''{{Cite web|和書|url=https://www.pref.yamanashi.jp/fujisan/rebirth/documents/fujisanmichi-omote.pdf|title=富士参詣富士山道表|accessdate=2019.02|publisher=山梨県富士山世界文化遺産保存活用推進協議会}}。 例として、北口本宮の境内図面から吉田口登山道が描かれた[[延宝]]8年（[[1680年]]）の『八葉九尊図』には現北口本宮境内が「下浅間」と記されている{{Cite journal|author=串田優子 伊藤裕久|year=2006|title=北口本宮冨士浅間神社境内空間の変遷過程|journal=日本建築学会計画系論文集|volume=第604号|page=159−16S}}。また、[[文化 (元号)|文化]]11年（[[1814年]]）に成立した甲斐国の地誌である『[[甲斐国志]]』にも、以下の記載がある。 {{Quotation|是古社殿ナキ以前富士浅間遥拝ノ地ニ築ク後神祠ヲ創造シ'''小室浅間明神'''ヲ勧請スト云}} {{Quotation|小室ヲ'''上浅間'''ト云此祠ヲ'''下浅間'''ト稱スルハ本小室ト同社ノ謂ナリトソ、又下吉田ニ浅間アリ是ヲハ'''下ノ宮浅間'''ト稱ス}} このことから、吉田口二合目の小室浅間神社（現・冨士御室浅間神社旧本宮）が「'''上浅間'''」、そこから勧請した上吉田の北口本宮が「'''下浅間'''」と呼ばれ、それとは別に下吉田の「'''下ノ宮浅間'''」があることがわかる。 上述のことから、「下浅間」と「下宮浅間」は別の存在であったが、下宮浅間から北口本宮に上吉田の氏子地域を譲ったこと、富士河口湖町勝山が管理する二合目の冨士御室浅間神社との関係が薄くなり、いつしか「上浅間」と呼ばれなくなったことで、代わりに北口本宮が上吉田の浅間神社「上浅間」、下吉田の浅間神社が「下浅間」と呼ばれるようになり、明治に小室浅間神社と改称したことなどから、近代以降に「下浅間」と「下宮浅間」が混同されていった。 == 祭事 == === 流鏑馬祭り === [[ファイル:小室浅間神社（下宮）神馬舎.jpg|thumb|200px|神馬舎と飼育されている神馬]] [[ファイル:Fujiyosida-Yabusame-FujisanSimomiyaOmurosengen.webm|thumb|富士吉田、冨士山下宮小室浅間神社の流鏑馬（2020年9月19日撮影）]] 山梨県無形民俗文化財に指定されている。 [[例祭]]は9月19日に行われ、「'''馬蹄占（ばていうらない）'''」をする[[流鏑馬]]神事が有名である。地元では「'''うまっとばし'''」や「'''うまとばしのお祭り'''」（馬をとばす（甲州弁）＝馬を走らせる（標準語））と呼ばれる。 [[長寛]]2年([[1164年]])中興馬乗りから始まったとされ、流鏑馬をすることが定められたのは[[安元]]2年([[1176年]])という。 朝馬、夕馬、切火などの流鏑馬祭の法式が定められたのが建久3年([[1192年]])、毎年9月19日に行う事が定められたのが永亨12年([[1440年]])と伝わる。 境内では流鏑馬に使う[[神馬]]が飼育されている。この馬は[[日本中央競馬会]]から奉納されたものである。 この例祭は一般的に知られる流鏑馬と異なり、農耕信仰及び土地の人々に密接した変わった流鏑馬神事で、世襲の「'''占人（うらびと）'''」が馬の足跡によって吉凶を占う「'''馬蹄占（ばていうらない）'''」、様々なことに神意を伺う為に引かれる「'''神籤（みくじ）'''」、「'''切火（きりひ）'''」と呼ばれる一週間に渡り身を清める[[潔斎]]が特徴的である。 馬蹄占いを目的としているため、弓矢を放つことや、的に当てる事は重要視されておらず、流鏑馬というより馬を走らせる祭事として、地元で呼ばれる「'''うまっとばし'''」の名前が的を得ている。[[ファイル:足跡を見て占う「占人」.jpg|サムネイル|特色である「'''馬蹄占（ばていうらない）'''」をする「'''占人（うらびと）'''」]]流鏑馬の馬は、氏子が馬主になって奉納するのが決まりであり、祭りは1月15日筒粥祭明けの馬主・奉仕馬申込と選定「馬出しのくじ占」から始まり、9月1日の「初馬揃」9月9日「中馬揃」9月13日「潔斎始」9月15日「後馬揃」9月18日「天神社への参向ならびに天神社山王祭」「例大祭宵宮祭」9月19日「例大祭流鏑馬祭」9月２０「後祭」以降、各町「お日待ち・秋葉講」と神事が続く。 かつて、自家で馬を飼育していない家では、馬を飼育する地内の家や他村の農家などに依頼し祭礼の期間だけ馬を借り受けていた。時代の流れと共に、馬を飼育している家もなくなり、現在では神社で馬を飼育して使用している。 かつては、富士山登山門と馬返しまでの概ね中間にあたる'''中の茶屋の近くにあった「騮ヶ馬場」'''{{Cite book|title=吉田口登山道の騮ヶ馬場と流鏑馬|date=2019.1.1|year=2019.1.1|publisher=山梨県立富士山世界遺産センター}} で行われていた。戦国時代ごろは河口湖と吉田の中間地点「'''長馬場'''」で近隣諸社合同行われていた。 神社に伝わる話によると、流鏑馬の主導を巡り村間の争いが激しくなっていったため、[[享禄]]3年（[[1530年]]）に[[武田氏]]の家臣である板垣信賢（※[[板垣信方]]のこと）の達により、各々の村で奉納されるようになったと云う。 現在の馬場「'''本町中村馬場'''」は江戸時代後期には既に使われていたことが嘉永元年（1848年）の「9月19日祭礼絵図」により分かっている。 [[ファイル:富士山神輿.JPG|200px|thumb|right|富士山神輿]][[2007年]]（平成19年）に、担ぎ手が不足し途絶えていた富士山神輿が半世紀ぶりに復活し、9月18日の宵祭りに神輿巡行が行われている。 ; 馬出しの神籤祭 : 1月15日早朝、筒粥祭の占いの結果が公表された後に、流鏑馬祭奉仕希望者の申込が行われ、正午から神事による奉仕馬のくじ引きが行われる。かつては6頭と定められた奉仕馬に、30から60頭もの申し込みがあった。その家から流鏑馬の奉仕馬・馬主を出すことは大変な名誉であった。近年では、定数以上の奉仕馬の申込が無く申込の受付のみで祭儀は行えていない。 ; 初馬揃祭 : 9月1日、例大祭に出る馬は全て神社に集まり、神事が行われる。各馬主は稽古鞍授与の神籤を引き、占人より稽古用の馬具一式を受け取る。その後、馬場見せ・馬場ならし・馬駆けを行う。（現在は、神社飼育の神馬で境内の馬場で練習等が行われている） ; 中馬揃祭 : 9月9日、奉仕馬が集まり、神事の後、馬場ならし・馬駆けを行う。 ; 潔斎始祭 : 9月13日、神事にて、木花咲耶姫命の御姿の軸、御幣などが授与される。流鏑馬馬主・奉仕者はこの日より神社境内の潔斎館に移り住み精進潔斎の生活に入る。かつては各馬主の自宅で行われており、妻をはじめ、奉仕者以外の家族全員を親戚縁者の家に出し、木花咲耶姫命の御姿の軸を祀った祭壇を設けて家を清め奉仕者や助勤者のみで男所帯の共同生活が行われていた。 ; 後馬揃祭 : 9月15日、各馬主は神馬の装飾を授与され、神事にて流鏑馬本番に使用する本鞍を選ぶ神籤を引き、結果によって占人よりそれぞれ本番用の馬具一式を受け取る。 ; 山王社宵宮祭 : 9月17日、馬主・奉仕者は山王社に参拝し弓取の儀が行われて、占人から儀式の伝授をうける。 ; 山王社祭・流鏑馬祭宵宮祭 : 9月18日、日中小室浅間神社より神職・占人・馬主・奉仕馬等、流鏑馬に関係する諸人が行列を組んで山王社への参向が行われ、富士山神輿が巡行する。 : [[ファイル:FujisanSimomiyaOmuroSengen O-mikujiRitual 宵祭り神籤神事.jpg|thumb|流鏑馬祭宵宮祭での神籤神事。神籤により流鏑馬祭本祭での役目と、神馬を走らせる順番が選定される]]その夜、宵宮祭が行われ、神籤により馬主ごとに「朝馬」「夕馬」の役馬の担当と神馬を走らせる順番が決められる。 : 祭礼を通して馬具は「占人」が管理しており、馬の額を飾る「'''オテンゴー'''、御天狗」は馬の鬣（タテガミ）を組紐で編んだもので、馬形埴輪の額に付された角状の飾りを継承したものと考えられており、祭礼当日早朝に「占人」が整える。[[ファイル:馬蹄占流鏑馬.jpg|サムネイル|278x278ピクセル|夕馬疾走、馬の額にある角状のものが「オテンゴー」]] ; 例大祭流鏑馬祭 : 9月19日、神事で矢、弓、的が馬主に渡され、「朝馬」「夕馬」の順番で流鏑馬をし、足跡による占い「馬蹄占」が行われる。最後に「山王さん（山王馬）」のノッパライ（乗り払い）が行われる。これは秋の収穫を見届けた山の神をヤマ（富士山）に送っていくからという。18日の「天神社への参向ならびに天神社山王祭」を行う下仲「天神社（山王社）」の伝承に「下宮の馬場をひと馬場借りて、山王さんのウマットバシをする」とあり、山王馬のノッパライとの係りが推測される。 ; 流鏑馬後祭 : 9月20日、流鏑馬「馬蹄占」の結果が報告され、ただちに各町に伝えられる。 ; お日待ち : 流鏑馬祭りが終わると、各町内に神職を招き「馬蹄占」の結果をもとに「お日待ち」と呼ばれる祭事を行う。 :小さなものでは近隣10軒くらい、大きなものでは自治会単位で食堂や個人宅、自治会館に集まり、祭神の掛け軸を飾り祭壇を設え、飲食を共にする。 :各家庭では、その後に神職から紙垂を1枚戴き、一年間火事や争い事がなく無事に過ごせるよう祈願する。 :戦前までは朝まで寝ずに談話して過ごし、日の出を拝んで解散していた。 === 筒粥祭 === [[ファイル:FujisanSimomiyaOmuroSengenShrine Kayu-ura Ritual.jpg|thumb|筒粥祭は深夜、世襲の占人一族（[[葭之池温泉|葭之池温泉一門]]）による筒粥保存会の奉仕で行われる]] 山梨県では当社をはじめ富士北麓地域や[[八ヶ岳]]山麓地域において筒粥神事が残されている。小室浅間神社の[[粥占|筒粥祭]]は、1月14日夜から翌日未明にかけて行われる[[神事]]。これにより年間の五穀豊穣・天候・[[養蚕]]・富士山登拝者数を占い、特にこの富士参詣者の多寡を占う点が特徴とされる勝俣（2007）、p.643。結果は筒粥占標として公表される。 また、筒粥神事の後には[[囲炉裏]]から[[釜]]を外し、[[燠]]（おき）の上で「カツノキ」と呼ばれる[[ヌルデ]]の樹で作られた駒を乗せ、その焼き具合で天候を占う「テリフリ占い」も行われる。こちらの結果も晴雨占標として公表される。 小室浅間神社の筒粥神事は戦国時代の富士北麓地域の年代記である『勝山記』にも「ツゝカイ」として記録されており、戦国時代の段階で占う14種の農作物とともに、ほぼ現在と一致する神事であったと考えられている勝俣（2007）、p.644。 筒粥神事にも世襲の「占人」一族（[[葭之池温泉|葭之池温泉一門]]）があり、神社の主な祭儀が占い神事で、それぞれに世襲の一族が代々奉仕していることが大変珍しい。 === 御更衣祭 === 60年に一度、[[祭神]]（[[コノハナサクヤビメ|木花咲耶姫命]]）の[[神体]]の着衣を替える「御更衣祭」が行われる。[[20世紀]]には[[戦後]]の[[1950年]]（昭和25年）に儀式が実施された。[[平成時代]]には[[2010年]]（平成22年）[[9月19日]]深夜2時に実施され、次回は[[2070年]]である。「御更衣祭」の時以外に神体を目にすると、必ず良くないことが起きると伝えられている。 === 神馬祭 === 例年、5月５日こどもの日に斎行される。「馬と子供のお祭り」として親しまれている。 主に農作業等に従事する働く馬や、歴代神馬への感謝と慰霊が行われ、地元商店会の出店やイベントで賑わう。 == 御神馬 == [[ファイル:冨士山下宮小室浅間神社 JRA奉納 神馬 瑞桜（ヒカリシャーク）.jpg|thumb|神馬 瑞桜（ヒカリシャーク）]] 馬蹄占をする流鏑馬祭り維持保存の為に、[[1993年]]（平成5年）より境内で御神馬を飼育している。 {| class="wikitable" |+歴代御神馬 ! !馬名 !神馬名 !備考 |- |1 |ヒカリシャーク |瑞桜（ずいおう） | |- |2 |マックスポート | | |- |3 |トーワタケシバ | | |- |4 |ダイイチヒジリ | | |- |5 |トキン | | |- |6 |イチエイクリッパー | | |- |7 |シロ | | |- |8 |キングズオブザサン |旺輝（おうき） | |- |９ |ワイズセレクション |賢旺（けんおう） |現任 |} 終身制で天寿を全うした歴代御神馬は神馬社に合祀されている。 毎年5月5日に神馬祭が行われている。 神馬舎では御神馬以外にも木曽馬、ポニーなどが複数飼育されている。 == 摂末社 == === 大塔宮社・雛鶴社 === * 祭神：[[護良親王|大塔宮護良親王]]・[[雛鶴神社|雛鶴姫]] * 例祭：5月10日（桂樹祭） [[ファイル:Ootounomiya-katura1.jpg|thumb|216px|本殿脇の御神木「大塔宮桂之古跡」の桂樹]] 境内、桂の御神木に祀られており「'''大塔宮桂之古跡'''」とも称し、「お桂さん」としても親しまれている。 [[南北朝時代 (日本)|南北朝時代]]、騒乱で討たれた[[大塔宮]]護良親王の首級を雛鶴姫が負って落ちのび、桂の御神木の根元に葬ったと古文書等で伝わる。 古文書の一つは、[[建武 (日本)|建武]]2年（[[1355年]]）[[9月23日]][[清和天皇]]遠孫某よりの祈請書の写し（原書は所在不明）で、下宮浅間の社地にある桂の神木の元に護良親王の首級を葬ったので、[[源義光|新羅三郎義光]]像を刻んで奉納し密かに[[護良親王]]として神木と共に祀る事を望むと記されている。 [[ファイル:Ootounomiya-katura2.jpg|thumb|右から雛鶴社・大塔宮社・首塚]] 桂の御神木は樹齢約800年で[[富士吉田市]][[天然記念物]]に指定されている。 === 神馬社 === * 祭神：白馬像で馬の御霊を祀る。 * 例祭：5月5日（神馬祭） 木花之開耶姫の乗り物の神馬と馬の御霊を祀る。 5月5日の神馬祭は「馬のお祭り」として親しまれており、地元商店の出店で賑わい、飼育している神馬を使った子供たちの体験乗馬等が行われている。 === 日枝社 === * 祭神：[[大山咋神]] * 例祭：5月5日 地元では「お猿さん」と云われ親しまれている。社殿に御使いの猿の神像が控えている。 === 五社神社（大神社・山神社・天王社・稲荷社・天神社） === * 祭神：天照皇大神・大山祇尊・須佐之男命・大己貴尊・少名彦尊・倉稲魂尊・菅原道真命 * 例祭：4月10日 五つの社を纏めた神社 === 室宮恵比寿社 === * 祭神：[[えびす|恵比寿]] * 例祭：11月19日夜 [[尾形光琳|尾形光琳彩]]色の恵比寿像を祀る。11月19日夜には[[恵比寿講]]が行われる。 === 胎内弁天社 === * 祭神：[[弁才天|弁財天]]
